# Canary — islam.museum release notes

The museum's public release notes: every change that lands on `main`, recorded in
reader's language in the same commit that makes the change. Newest release first.
The site build reads the version and date from the top block below and shows them
in the footer of every page and on the changelog page (`/{lang}/changelog/`).

Rules for every agent and contributor (`docs/engineering/15-release-notes-and-versioning.md`):
append your entry under the current version block, grouped by kind — Added, Changed,
Fixed, Removed, Performance, Tests, Data, Breaking, Rolled back. Write what changed
and why it matters, never a bare commit message. If your change bumps the version,
open a new block on top with the new version and today's date.

---

## v2.31.0 — 2026-11-24
### Added
- **Granada palace evaluation LOD exports in the games workshop (not on the site).** The Candidate C palace Blender script can now export separate `palace-lod1` and `palace-lod2` evaluation files with the same origin, axes, scale and `palace` node name, fewer procedural segments and eight runtime material groups. The files are local evaluation artifacts only, outside git and not loaded by any game; the palace remains a reconstruction with historical review pending, not accepted or production art.
- **A public-domain vegetation survey for the Granada game evaluation (documentation only, not on the site).** The games workshop now records candidate CC0 sources for olive, cypress, citrus, poplar, fig, vine, wheat, vegetables, reeds and hedging, with licence locations, species confidence, published triangle/material/texture/download figures where the sources state them, required retopology/LOD/wind work and gaps such as the missing pomegranate tree. Nothing was downloaded, bought, contacted, imported or approved; the survey is evidence for a later owner decision.
- **The occasions-and-society wave: ten new class-driven browsers, in seven languages.** Ten more front doors over the one graph on the shelves pattern (`scripts/shelves.ts` + `site/src/components/sig/ShelfPage.astro`, membership computed from the records themselves at build time): `/[lang]/aayad/` (Islamic Festivals and Occasions — Ramadan, the two Eids, Hajj and its rites, the Kaaba ceremonies, the rites of life, death and war, observances, the sacred months, customs, foods and regional variations past and present), `/[lang]/himam/` (People of Determination — disability in the record: the companions and scholars who lived blind, deaf, lame or palsied, the fiqh accommodations and the sunnah), `/[lang]/zakat/` (Zakat and Sadaqat — the third pillar as institution: the eight asnaf, nisab and hawl, the treasury and taxes, history, works and fatwas), `/[lang]/itq/` (Freeing the Enslaved — the freed and their stories, itq/mukataba/tadbir rulings and the equality of the farewell sermon), `/[lang]/hukm/` (Governance in Islam — the caliphate, viziers, governors, diwans, judges and mazalim, hisba and shurta, ahkam sultaniyya works and the madhhabs), `/[lang]/atfal/` (Children in Islam — the child companions and prodigies and the child's rights: aqiqa, milk and hadhana, nafaqa, the orphan's wealth, tarbiya and taklif), `/[lang]/masakin/` (The Poor and the Underdog — ahl al-suffa and the beaten converts, poverty concepts and the sunnah's promises) `/[lang]/dukhul/` (Entering Islam — the converts and their conversion events, modern reverts, those who left and the apostate-prophets, and the shahada/kufr/ridda rulings) `/[lang]/maadin/` (Metals, Money and the Wealthy — gold, silver, minerals, dinars and the sakk, jewellery, the rich companions and a'yan, Qarun and the morality stories; the counterpart of masakin) and `/[lang]/muamalat/` (Transactions and Personal-Status Fiqh — inheritance and the will, marriage and its prohibitions, contracts and riba/qimar, lawful food, intoxicants, punishments, and the fatwas classified by domain). Each ships its page in all seven languages, the filter, the filter index row, an Explore menu entry, `/api/v1/<slug>.json` (OpenAPI + `llms.txt`), plan documents (87–96) and acceptance specs (80–89).
- **The festivals content wave: 26 new records and ~90 records tagged in place.** New `practice` records with trilingual prose and cited sources — Eid customs and foods (takbir, eidi, greetings, clothes, kahk, maamoul, qatayef, sheer khurma, sambousek, haleem, ketupat), Ramadan customs (fanous, musaharati, gargee'an, mahya, mudik, chaand raat, iftar cannon), Kaaba and Hajj ceremonies (kiswa change, ghusl al-Kaaba, the mahmal, halq, ramy al-jamarat), regional rites (zaffa, jashn-e-taklif, arba'een) — plus six new zakat-recipient `concept` records (the eight asnaf of Q 9:60) and `group/bani-shayba` for the keepers of the Kaaba key; ~90 existing records (grief, talaq, Hijra, Muwatta zakat chapters, Mutanabbi's Eid poems, kiswa and key objects, hadith chapters of the occasions) tagged into their sections. ~22 new Wikipedia/Al-Jazeera/NatGeo source records.
- **Groundwork for a games section, nothing visible yet.** The museum is to have a set of browser games (the founder's specification of 25 November 2026). This change adds the workshop for them and no page: a separate `gaming/` workspace that the museum's own build never touches, a written inventory of how the site is built and hosted, the decisions taken so far with their evidence, a threat model for player-made content, and a first graphics test. The test draws one invented riverside city (770 buildings) in two 3D engines on WebGPU and measures them in Chrome on one Apple M4 Max; Three.js was chosen. The real screenshots are in `docs/gaming/evidence/m1/` and are plainly simpler than the concept art; the report says where. No game exists, nothing is on the site, and nothing is translated because there is nothing yet for a visitor to read. Details: `docs/gaming/README.md`.
- **Atlas, the first game, as a prototype (not on the site yet).** A daily geography game in the games workshop: five rounds, each naming a museum record (an event, or a historical figure's birth or death) and asking where it happened; turn a globe, drop a pin, see how far off you were, and follow the link to the record. Every question is a museum record joined to a museum place, with nothing written or guessed by the game; a pinned pack of 2,125 rounds in 528 places gives 365 days with no question asked twice, and that schedule is checked by the tests. It plays by mouse or by keyboard alone, in the museum's seven languages, right to left for Arabic and Urdu. It is a prototype: no images, no sound, a flat-coloured globe, interface strings no native speaker has read, and no person has played it yet. Building it counted what the museum's records can support: 1,073 places still have only approximate coordinates, and Turkish and Indonesian names are missing for people. Details: `docs/gaming/games/atlas.md`.
- **Rules for the city-building game, tested before anything is drawn (not on the site).** The Golden Age, the second game in the workshop, now has the rules of its first scenario: a district on a river where water, food, work, money, learning and welfare depend on what is built where, played a season at a time. There is nothing to see or play yet. What there is instead is a test bench that played 14,000 whole campaigns with fourteen scripted players: no rule broke, and nobody won by doing nothing, by taxing, or by building one thing over and over. It also found that only two of four sensible strategies win reliably, where the design asks for three, and that is written down as an open problem and not hidden. Details: `docs/gaming/games/golden-age.md`.
- **The Golden Age can now be played, as a prototype (not on the site yet).** The city-building game in the games workshop has its first scenario, "The Failing Canal", on screen: a riverside district drawn in 3D from the state of the game, where you dig canal links and watch the water arrive, place nine kinds of building, set the tax, choose research and end the season. Beside each stock the top bar shows what the season will do to it before you commit, and a ledger gives the reasons afterwards, down to each point of welfare. The same game can be played with the keyboard alone or from a plan view made of buttons, which is the whole game in a browser without WebGPU. It saves on the device, and it is in seven languages (all written by AI agents; none read yet by a native speaker). The author's script has played it through in Chrome in every language; no person has played it, and the picture is a tidy model town, not the concept art.
- **The museum's own music in the games.** Both games in the workshop, Atlas and The Golden Age, now play "Voices of the Museum", the museum's six-track suite, from one shared player: silent until your first click, with a switch, a volume control and a "next track" button, and a line saying what the suite is (fully AI-generated, composed around the founder's oud playing, as the Backstage page says) with a link to that page. Turning the music off in one game turns it off in all of them. The audio files are not in the repository, by the rule that media lives on R2; a record of what was imported, with a digest of each file, is.
- **The Golden Age shows where the trouble is, and points to the museum (still a prototype, not on the site).** A plot whose building is not doing its job now carries a marker in the district (no water in reach, or no houses to serve) and is listed in the panel as a button that takes you there; silt turns the canals brown until it is cleared, and a drought lowers the river. Each research project and most tools name the museum record of the real thing behind the idea (the norias of Hama for the water wheel, Samarkand paper, the Nizamiyya madrasas, the market inspector, Harun al-Rashid's bimaristan and eight more) and link to it in your language; the district itself stays fictional and says so.
- **A second chapter for The Golden Age: "The House of Books" (still a prototype, not on the site).** After the failing canal, the district is asked to become a place of learning: paper has arrived, so the library can be built from the first season, but schools and libraries must be paid for, half the households have no work, and the canal carries less than a larger district needs. Each chapter now opens on a brief that says what is asked and then quotes the museum's own account of the real history behind it (Samarkand paper and the Nizamiyya madrasas for this chapter; al-Mansur's water conduits and al-Karaji's levelling for the first), in your language and with a link to the record. The game adds no historical sentence of its own. Scripted players won the new chapter in four different ways across 14,000 games; no person has played it.
- **A third chapter for The Golden Age, "What Endures", and a rule of its own: endowments (still a prototype, not on the site).** The district is prosperous and fevers come with the caravans; you are asked to make its welfare last. From this chapter a school, bath, library or hospital can be endowed: a sum is set aside for ever, its upkeep is paid from then on, and it can no longer be cleared, the game's form of the waqf. The chapter cannot be won without four. Its brief quotes the museum's records of Ibn Tulun's endowed hospital and of the waqf supervisor. Scripted players won it in four different ways across 14,000 games, but one of them, the trading city, never lost and ended rich each time: that is recorded as a fault in the game's economy to be repaired, not hidden. A game saved before this change still loads. No person has played the chapter.
- **Atlas gets no picture rounds yet, and the count that says why (games workshop, not on the site).** The geography game was to gain rounds that show a photograph and ask where it is. Before building them, the rule for which of the museum's pictures may be used was written down: a real photograph, under a free licence with its author credited, of something the museum ties to exactly one place whose coordinates are exact enough to score a guess, with no person pictured, no manuscript page, no AI image and nothing marked sensitive; before the guess the page shows only the author and the licence, and the full credit comes with the answer. The museum's 895 media records were then counted against that rule, and four qualify. The museum's pictures are almost all of objects, inventions and ideas: one of its 1,908 exactly located places and seven of its 5,794 buildings have a picture at all. One picture round a week needs 52, so none was built, and nothing in the game changed. The rule is kept as tested code with a command that takes the count again, and the decision record lists which records would change the answer and four questions for the founder (`docs/gaming/adr/G-0008-atlas-image-rounds.md`).
- **Granada, an eleventh game, begins with its arithmetic (games workshop, not on the site, not playable).** The founder's design for a strategy game set in a kingdom inspired by Nasrid Granada in 1475 (water, farming, trade, building) was read in full and filed, and a report says what the museum can and cannot yet support it with. The first thing built is what a player will never see and every screen will depend on: the money and the goods. They are whole numbers that only ever move from one account to another, so nothing can be counted twice or paid twice. A market has one price for buying and a lower one for selling, and only as much money as it has. A harvest too big for the store asks what to do with the rest instead of losing it quietly. A contract sets aside what it needs and pays once. The design's own concept pictures contain four mistakes of this kind (an olive crop valued at the price of oil, two ports drawn side by side that are 175 km apart with inland Granada between them, a price table that would hand out free money, food called adequate at 91% of its target); each is now a test that fails if the mistake comes back. The places are the museum's own records with the museum's coordinates. What the museum does not yet have for this game (the crops of the Vega and their seasons, the canals, the silk trade, the coinage) is listed, and nothing historical is shown to anyone until a record supports it. There is no screen: this is a foundation, tested by 60,000 random commands and by breaking it on purpose fifteen ways to see that the tests notice.
- **The games now have their own way out of the workshop, separate from the museum's pages (nothing is live yet).** Until now a game could only be run on a developer's machine. The games can now be built into a release, checked, and published on their own, without rebuilding or redeploying a single museum page, and the museum's own build and deployment no longer run when only a game changes. A release is a small folder of files, each named by a fingerprint of its content and listed in a manifest with its size and checksum; it is stored once and never altered, and making it live, or going back to the one before, changes one tiny pointer file. The games will be served from an address of their own (games.islam.museum, with a test copy at uat-games.islam.museum), so a fault in a game cannot touch the museum's pages; the server there sends strict security rules with every file, under which a page may load only from its own address. Both existing games were opened in a real browser under those rules, in Arabic and English, without a fault. Publishing remains the founder's own step, test copy first, and **it has not been taken**: this change adds the machinery and runs none of it against the live hosting. The museum's site is to gain a Play page that leads to the games; that is not in this change either.
- **Granada's first chapter exists as rules: "Water for the Valley" (games workshop, not on the site, nothing to see yet).** A valley district is now lived a day at a time: water comes down from the river into a pool and out along branches to the fields and the households, and when there is not enough the steward says who drinks first; a field grows as fast as it is watered and tended, and thirst costs it part of its crop; a ripe field is carried in by hand, a little each day, into a store that may be full, and what will not fit waits in the field or is sold there, never quietly lost; households eat, fare well or badly, and arrive or leave. The steward can mend a broken water branch cheaply or rebuild and extend it at a price, sow, build a house or a granary, and trade at a market with two prices. Five tasks are checked by the rules themselves, not by a button: water reaching the olive terrace, the first harvest brought in, food held for winter, a new household housed, room made in the store. The weather of every day is fixed when a game begins, so the forecast the game will show is what really happens unless the player acts. Six scripted players have played the chapter 6,000 times without breaking a rule; one that does nothing never wins, and its failures exposed two tasks that could be completed by neglect, which were rewritten. It is honest to say what this is not: there is no screen yet, so no person can play it, and the chapter is too forgiving as it stands (two of the four sensible ways of playing cannot lose). The crops and their seasons are game elements; the museum has no record yet of what the Vega of Granada grew.
- **A first try at a better palace for the Granada game, and an honest stop (games workshop; not on the site).** After the founder's decision that neither set of buildings would do, a palace was written as one building of its own: an uneven ring of walls and towers, two courts with arcades of horseshoe arches, a pool, a bath, a garden and a gate, with wear painted into its walls. It is far richer than what the prototype shows, and from a distance it reads as a palace; near to, it still looks built from boxes. The founder's own rule for that case is to stop and come back to him with a proposal for an artist and for licensed plants, and that is what was done. It is not in the game.
- **The founder's decision on the Granada game's art is recorded (games workshop; not on the site).** Two sets of buildings had been made for the game by script: the one in the prototype, and a more detailed second set by another agent. The founder accepted neither as the look of the finished game. The first stays in the prototype for now, the second is kept as an experiment and not merged, and a new attempt at one complete view is to be made and brought to him to judge before any building is made in number. The record says plainly that no artist is engaged and that the developer is an AI that models by writing scripts. Nothing a visitor sees has changed.
- **Granada can be played (a prototype in the games workshop; not on the site, and not yet in 3D).** The first chapter, "Water for the Valley", now opens as a page: a bar across the top shows the valley as it is (money, days of food, households, welfare, the water in the pool, the room in the store), and under it a line says what tomorrow and the next ten days will bring if you do nothing more, which is the game's own rules run ahead, not an estimate. A drawn plan shows the river, the pool, the channel and its branches (water moving along the ones that flow, a red cross on the broken one), the three fields as they grow, ripen and are gathered, a house for every ten households, the store filling, and the snow mountain under the museum's own name for it. Tabs hold the fields, the works, the market with its two prices, and what happened yesterday. You can let the days pass, hurry them, stop them, or take them one at a time; the game is kept on your device and comes back to the same day. It is in Arabic, English, Urdu, French, Spanish, Turkish and Indonesian, every control can be reached by keyboard, and in Arabic and Urdu the panels change sides while the land keeps east on the right. An opening note says plainly that this is a game and not a history, and links to what the museum holds on Granada. A script has played it through to the end in a real browser in each of the seven languages. What it is not, yet: the lit, three-dimensional valley the design calls for is the next piece of work, the five translations other than Arabic and English were made by machine and none of the seven has been read by a native speaker, and no person has played it.
- **The games' first trial deployment (to the test copy only; nothing is on the public site).** The three prototype games, Granada first, were published for the first time through the games' own route to the museum's test copy, at an address of their own that search engines are told to ignore and that nothing links to. It took two minutes: the small server for the games was created, the 46 files were uploaded, read back and checked one by one against their recorded fingerprints, and only then switched on. Granada was then opened there in Arabic and played for three days without a fault. This proves the separate route works end to end on the real hosting; it does not put any game before the public. The public address is not deployed, and going back to an earlier release has not been tried there yet, because there is only one.
- **Granada's valley can be seen in 3D (a prototype in the games workshop; not on the site).** The first chapter of Granada was played from panels and a flat plan. It now also opens on a valley you can move through: the river, the pool and its channels, the three fields with their crops, the village, olive terraces, a walled hill town and a snow range behind it, under the light of the season, with blossom in spring and gold poplars in autumn. It shows the same game as the plan: water runs in a branch only when the branch can carry it, wheat thins as it is brought in, a house appears when it is built. Every shape is generated by the game's own code; no picture is downloaded and the founder's concept image is used nowhere. It is honest to say how far it is from that image: the trees are rounded shapes, the houses are boxes, the people glide. It needs a browser with WebGPU and falls back to the plan without it, and it has been measured on one fast computer only (120 frames a second there). The panels are now teal with gold lines. No person other than its author has seen it.
- **Atlas's globe is now a lit sphere (a prototype in the games workshop; not on the site).** The geography game drew its globe as a flat disc of coastlines. Where the browser has WebGPU the Earth is now a sphere under a light, with the sea, the land, a paler edge of water along the coasts, a shell of air and stars behind; the pins and the line from your guess to the place are drawn over it exactly where they were, which tests hold to the pixel. It shows coastlines only, with no borders or names (as before) and no mountains, because the game has no elevation data. Nothing is downloaded for it and no photograph of the Earth is used. Without WebGPU the drawn globe remains and the game is the same.
- **The games' test copy now shows Granada's valley and Atlas's globe in 3D (the test copy only; nothing is on the public site).** The third trial release of the games carries both. Opened there in a browser, all three prototypes start in 3D with the museum's music and no error. A page for asking an outside reviewer to try them was added, with the three addresses and a note that the other eight games are not built.
- **Granada's village looks like a village of al-Andalus (a prototype in the games workshop; not on the site).** The valley's houses were plain boxes. They are now lime-washed houses under clay-tile roofs, with doors, shutters, chimneys and walled yards; a mosque with a square minaret stands by the square; a watermill stands on the west channel and its wheel turns only while that channel carries water; a stone bridge of three arches takes a new road over the river; ox-carts go along the roads; and the people lean from foot to foot as they walk. All of it is still generated by the game's own code, and it is still far from the founder's concept image. The mill is scenery for now: the game has no milling until its second act.
- **An outside audit of the games, taken as the plan of work (games workshop; nothing on the site).** The founder had the games' documents audited against his own specifications by an outside reviewer, who returned fourteen pieces of corrective work: production-quality art and a real trading economy for Granada, a fix for a city-building chapter that one strategy always wins, unfair rounds in the geography game, human playtests, the eight games not yet built, and more. The audit is kept as received, its findings were checked against the repository, and one generated page now shows every acceptance gate beside the work that bears on it. The reviewer could not open the games itself, and says so; no gate was passed by this.
- **A workshop for the games' art, and the first thing made in it (games workshop; nothing on the site, nothing in a game yet).** Until now every building in the games was put together from plain boxes in the visitor's browser. Buildings can now be made ahead of time by scripts run in Blender: modelled in real metres with bevelled edges, covered in textures painted by the same scripts (plaster, clay tile, coursed stone, planks), and exported for a game to load. The first is a watermill for Granada, with a wheel that can turn. It exists as a rendered preview only; the game still draws its older, simpler mill. No photograph and no downloaded model or texture is used, and a record of checksums says exactly what the scripts made.
- **The games' test copy now shows Granada's village (the test copy only; nothing is on the public site).** The fourth trial release of the games carries the tiled village, the mosque with its minaret, the watermill and the bridge. Opened there in a browser in English and in Arabic, every game starts in 3D with the museum's music and no error.
- **Granada's valley can show the watermill made in Blender (games workshop; not on the site, and not on the test copy yet).** The valley now fetches the modelled mill and sets it down where its simpler, code-made mill stood, wheel in the channel, turning only while the channel carries water. The simpler mill is drawn first and stays if the model cannot be had, so the game never waits on a download and never breaks for want of one. The models are kept beside the games like the music, and none has been uploaded to a host yet.
- **The geography game no longer marks you wrong for knowing the answer (games workshop; not on the site).** Atlas asks where an event happened and scores the pin against the museum's record. Some records tie a battle to the nearest city and not to its field, so a player who pinned the place the question named lost points for it. An event named for a place is now asked only when one of its names, in any of the seven languages, is the name of the place it is scored at. 263 events are held back until their records are looked at, and are listed for the people who keep those records; none of the museum's data was changed. The year of daily games is still complete, and it does not ask more battles than before.
- **The games' models can travel to their host (games workshop; nothing on the site).** Buildings made in the art workshop are kept out of the repository, as the music is. They can now be carried to the games' host by the same guarded route: only the files a reviewed list names, each checked byte for byte, placed where only a model's files can go, and never written over.
- **The watermill's files are on the games' test copy (the test copy only; nothing on the public site).** The mill made in the art workshop was carried to the test host by the guarded route and read back from it identical to the record of what was made. The game on the test copy does not show it yet: that takes the next trial release.
- **The games' test copy now shows the watermill made in Blender, and the geography game's fair rounds (the test copy only; nothing on the public site).** The fifth trial release is the first built to look for the modelled mill beside it. Opened there in a browser in English and in Arabic, Granada's valley takes the mill up and every game starts in 3D with no error.
- **The games can be handed to an outside tester who has no internet (games workshop; nothing on the site).** A reviewer's browser could not reach the test copy, so the same build can now be packed with everything it fetches, a small launcher and a guide, and played on one computer with the network off. The package is made from the build exactly as released, checked against its own record, and tried in a browser with all outside access cut off before it is handed over.
- **The geography game's globe no longer seems to vanish between rounds (games workshop; not on the site).** An outside reviewer playing the test copy found that after one round the next opened on a blank beige screen until the page was reloaded. The globe was still there: the game had stayed zoomed in on the last answer, far inland, where nothing but land was in view. Every round now begins from the whole globe, lines of latitude and longitude show over land as well as sea so that no view is empty, and the Home key returns to the whole globe. It is the first fault in the games found by someone other than their author.
- **The games were played by an outside reviewer for the first time, and its report is on file (games workshop; nothing on the site).** An AI reviewer driving a browser on the founder's own computer played all three games on the test copy from start to finish. It confirmed most of what had been claimed, could not make out two small things (carts on the roads, the way people walk), and found one real fault, since fixed. Its report, twelve proposals for turning the prototypes into finished games, a set of standards and two more target pictures are kept as received. It is a machine's review and not a person's; no game is called finished because of it, and each is still marked a prototype.
- **Every release of the games is now put through the outside reviewer's own steps (games workshop; nothing on the site).** A new tool plays, on the test copy itself, the parts of the reviewer's checklist that a script can play: the five addresses with and without 3D, and a whole day of the geography game by mouse, keyboard and typed coordinates, with no reload to hide a fault. Its 43 scenarios are listed with what covers each: 16 fully, 17 in part, 10 not yet. The reviewer's two games of the city-builder's third chapter (a trading city that only taxes ends rich and does not win) are kept as tests. The sixth release to the test copy, which carries the geography game's fix, passed these steps.
- **The founder's decisions on what the three games must become are recorded, with a plan to get there (games workshop; nothing on the site).** His three target pictures are now binding for what each game shows and does. A list sets out the 58 systems the pictures show: 3 exist today, 29 in part, 26 not at all. He set how long the games should last (three hours or more for the two strategy games), which computers and browsers they must run well on, and that people, not AI, review the history and test the play. A ledger now lists every statement of history the games make, all awaiting a human reviewer. A plan orders the work in six streams. All three games stay marked as prototypes, and a test now guards the label.
- **Going back to an earlier version of the games was rehearsed on the test copy, and it works (games workshop; nothing on the site).** With the founder's approval for one rehearsal, the test copy was moved back to its previous version and forward again. Both moves took about a minute, the earlier version was live for under four minutes, games already in progress carried on in both directions, and nothing was lost. The founder's further decisions are recorded as well: who must still be found (historians to review the history, people with two ordinary laptops to measure speed, and testers), what the first proof picture of each game must show, and which map data may be used for the globe. None of those people is named yet, and the record says so.
- **The games now say on their own pages that their history has not yet been reviewed (games workshop; not on the site, and not yet on the test copy).** Wherever a game links or quotes the museum's records, it now carries the words "historical review pending", in all seven languages. The city-builder describes itself, in the founder's words, as a fictional city inspired by records of Abbasid Baghdad, and no longer calls the museum's summaries "the real history". A test keeps the words in place until named historians have reviewed each game.
- **The table of map data for the globe was corrected after NASA's usage rules were read (games workshop; a document only).** NASA's rules allow its imagery in educational simulations with credit. The proposal is unchanged: land and relief from two public-domain sources, cloud drawn by the game, and no modern city lights while a question is open, because they can give the answer away.
- **The test copy of the games now carries the "historical review pending" wording (games workshop; not on the site).** The seventh release to the test copy was checked there: the wording shows in all three games, and every automated step passes. The automated steps now look for that wording on every release.
- **The games can now measure what they cost a computer (games workshop; nothing a player sees).** Opened with a special address, a game counts how long every frame takes, how much memory it uses and how many of each thing that can leak is alive. An ordinary game is not instrumented. The first reading of the Granada game was taken on the developer's own machine, which is far faster than the two ordinary laptops the founder has set as the test; no claim about speed is made from it.
- **The Granada game's houses are now modelled buildings with photographed plaster, roof tile and stone (games workshop; not on the site).** About two hundred houses in the valley, the village and the hill town are four authored designs with tiled roofs, shuttered windows and arched doors, in place of plain blocks. The surfaces are public-domain photographs from Poly Haven. It is a first step toward the founder's target picture and still far from it: the town is sparse, the land and trees are unchanged, and nothing here has been reviewed by a historian.
- **The Granada game's hill now has a stone wall with towers and a gate, builders' scaffolding and a crane, and a walled palace on its top; an olive estate stands by the terrace (games workshop; not on the site).** These are modelled buildings in place of plain blocks. The palace is a general picture of a fortified palace and copies no real building; nothing here has been reviewed by a historian, and the game says so. The camera can now travel as far as the lower town. The picture is still far from the founder's target: bare slopes, simple trees, no people.
- **The Granada game's lower town is now a real town of streets (games workshop; not on the site).** About three hundred houses stand in eight streets that curve round the hill below the palace wall, each facing down the slope, with cypresses and gardens between them, where a hundred and fifty had been scattered at random. A fault was fixed on the way: trees no longer grow through houses.
- **The Granada game's screen is rearranged round the valley, as in the founder's target picture (games workshop; not on the site).** In 3D the valley now fills the whole page. A rail on the left opens the game's parts, the steward's tasks stand beside it, the part in hand (the market, the fields, the works) stands on the right, and the season with the weather to come stands in the corner. A field chosen in the valley shows a small card beside it with what grows there and what can be done. Every panel does something; nothing is drawn for show. On a small window, or on the flat plan, the panels stand in one column as before.
- **A harvest in the Granada game now has people in it (games workshop; not on the site).** When a harvest is ordered, a line of reapers works across the wheat with stooks of cut corn behind them, or pickers climb ladders into the olive trees with baskets beneath; carriers walk to the store or the estate. They appear because the harvest was ordered and leave when it is done. The figures are simple ones, not yet modelled people.
- **The Granada game's trees have fuller crowns and a leafy surface (games workshop; not on the site).** Each tree is made of more and smaller heads, so its outline is irregular as a real tree's is, and its crown is dappled with light and shade in place of a smooth rounded shape. It costs more to draw; on the developer's fast machine it makes no difference to speed, and the two ordinary laptops the founder has named have not been tried.
- **The Granada game checked on its test address in all seven languages (games workshop; not on the site).** The check of the game's systems on the test address, run until now in English and Arabic, was also run in Urdu, French, Spanish, Turkish and Indonesian on the current test release, and passed in each. The translations themselves are by machine and have been read by no person. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **An hour's run of the Granada game, and the record of eight hours' work on it (games workshop; not on the site).** The game was played by its test tool for an hour on the developer's machine: sixty-two game years, no error, memory between 173 and 205 MB. Another program was open on the machine, most of the slow frames fell in five minutes that are not explained, and it is not the test on the founder's minimum machines, which a named person has still to run. The games' ledger now lists what the eight hours did, what they did not, and what waits for the founder. (Corrected the same day: that list had counted another agent's change to the site's footer among the games' own, and had given the game 433 strings where it has 432.) The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **The Granada game no longer loses the keyboard in two places (games workshop; not on the site).** A new test plays a year of the game with the keyboard alone. It found that after the opening text was closed, and after the year's question was answered, the keyboard was left on nothing; both are mended. Every control on each of the game's five parts is reached by the Tab key, in English and Arabic. The test is not a screen reader, and no person who relies on a keyboard has tried the game. It remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **An accessibility scan for the Granada game (games workshop; not on the site).** A new tool checks the game's page by machine, in English and Arabic, in each of thirty-two states a player meets, against the accessibility rules a machine can test. The first run found no rule broken. That is a net for one kind of fault and not a statement that the game is accessible: no person who uses a screen reader has tried it. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **Twenty-six faults in the Granada game mended after an independent review (games workshop; not on the site).** An automated reviewer had read the day's changes and found faults the author's own tests had not, two of them serious: a saved game could be overwritten after a rollback to an older version, and goods sent in the last days of the last year were never paid for. Both are mended, with twenty-four smaller ones, among them a way out of Photo Mode for players without a keyboard and building by keyboard alone on the plan. Five smaller faults found by the same review were mended afterwards in the same change: a question to the player now appears on the morning of its own day, and a moved price is a whole number of dinars. Four more, found by the reviewer in this change itself, were mended before it was merged: three concern a saved game after a rollback, which is now never written over, even when the device has no room for a copy. The prompt for a second agent working on the buildings' finish was rewritten in full. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **A long-run test for the Granada game, and three small faults mended (games workshop; not on the site).** A new tool plays the game for as long as asked and writes down each minute how fast it draws and how much memory it holds; it is the script for the hardware tests that named people will run on the founder's minimum machines. Ten minutes of it on the developer's machine found nothing leaking, and showed that one of the game's own counters had been over-counting, which is corrected. A review also mended a click that could reach behind Photo Mode, and signed figures that were shown back to front in Arabic and Urdu. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **The Granada game has a third year, "A Dry Year" (games workshop; not on the site).** A player who wins the second year can go on to a year in which the river runs low and little rain falls. It asks for two cisterns, for the households to be kept faring well for sixty days together, and for trade and the winter's food to be kept up all the same. The year and its figures are invented and say so. Its balance is a first attempt, and three short years are still far from the campaign length the founder has set. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **Goods now take time to travel in the Granada game (games workshop; not on the site).** A load sent to the port is three days on the road: its carriage is paid as it leaves, and it is sold, or delivered on its contract, on the morning it arrives, at that morning's price. The page lists what is on the road and says by when a contract's goods must leave to arrive in time. The game's ledger keeps every load in its books while it travels. Three days is a number chosen for play, not taken from a source. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **The Granada game's help now explains what was added to it (games workshop; not on the site).** Six short lines in the help cover the warnings, building, trade, choosing things on the land, Photo Mode, going on to the next year, and the keys. The page that records where the game stands was also corrected: it had still described the game as it was a day earlier. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **The Granada game now says what one year hands to the next, and its newest parts have been checked on the test address itself (games workshop; not on the site).** From autumn the game warns if nothing is sown for the spring of the year that follows, and at a won year's end it lists what goes on: the households, the money, the food and what is in the ground. A new check opens the game on the test address and tries the contract, building, the decision, Photo Mode and the second year under that address's own security rules; all passed in English and Arabic. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **The Granada game has a second year (games workshop; not on the site).** A player who wins the first year can go on to "The Merchants of Málaga" with the valley as they left it: its people, its store, its buildings, even the wheat sown in autumn. The second year asks for trade, a contract kept with the port, more households and a cistern. Testing over a thousand years of weather shows it can be won in more than one way and never by doing nothing, but its balance is a first attempt, and two short years are still far from the campaign length the founder has set. The port's contracts and figures are invented and say so. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **Buildings in the Granada game can now be chosen, and olive oil can be followed from grove to port (games workshop; not on the site).** A click on the store, the market, the estate or any building the player has placed opens a card with its own figures. A new card in the economy shows the oil's road in five steps, each with what stands there now and the next thing to do. A fault that put such cards partly off the page in Arabic and Urdu was found and fixed. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **The Granada game now warns of what lies ahead (games workshop; not on the site).** The overview lists what will go wrong if nothing more is done, soonest first: the day the households go hungry or short of water, a crop that will spoil, a contract that will fail, a winter reserve too small. Each line is the game's own rules run forward, and tests show each comes true on the day it names. The market says how much food can be spared, and the season is given in figures. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **Prices now move in the Granada game (games workshop; not on the site).** A market pays and asks less for a good it holds more of than usual and more for one it is short of, by up to fifteen parts in a hundred, and returns to its usual stock of itself. Each good says in words whether its price is above or below yesterday's. The top bar shows what trade has brought in the last thirty days. The size of the movement was chosen, and tested, so that buying and selling in a circle can never make money. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **The Granada game shows its region (games workshop; not on the site).** A small diagram places Granada, Málaga, Almería and the Sierra Nevada where the museum's own coordinates put them, with a scale and the straight-line distance to the port, and three layers lay the game's own figures over it: trade, fields and works. It is a diagram of true positions, not a drawn map: no country's outline is shown and the coast is only sketched. The game's valley and its trade are marked as invented. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **The Granada game has a Photo Mode (games workshop; not on the site).** In the 3D valley a visitor can put the whole page away, move the camera freely, choose a lens, preview another season, rain or a morning, midday or evening light for the picture alone, and save the view as an image. The game stands still meanwhile and nothing in it changes, which a test confirms. It can be used by keyboard alone and Escape always leaves. Checked by script on one machine; not yet on the minimum machines, and not yet tried by a person. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **The Granada game now asks the player a question with a price on each side, and keeps a journal (games workshop; not on the site).** In summer the village downstream asks for water: sharing brings money and less water for twenty days; keeping it costs the households' goodwill for twenty days. Each answer's cost is shown in figures before it is chosen, and the game's forecast already counts what will follow. A journal in the ledger keeps what has happened, day by day. The village and its request are invented and labelled so, with historical review pending. Testing shows the two answers are not yet evenly weighted. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **Each field in the Granada game now tells its own story in figures (games workshop; not on the site).** A field's card says who is tending it, what thirst has cost, how much it will give and in how many days, whether the store has room, and what the harvest is worth in the village and at the port. The forecast is the game's own rules run forward, and tests show it comes true to the unit and the day. A field can also be put first for water and workers when either is short. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **Buildings can be placed on the land in the Granada game (games workshop; not on the site).** The player chooses a house, a granary, a cistern or a garden and then its ground, in the 3D valley or on the plan, by mouse or by keyboard alone. A ring shows where it would stand and the game says in words why ground is refused: water, a field, a road, a steep slope, trees, or something already there. Building takes money, materials and days of work, and each building does one thing when it is finished. Games saved earlier are carried forward. In seven languages, machine-translated; the buildings are simple shapes and their history is marked as pending review. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **The Granada game has a port, an olive press and a contract (games workshop; not on the site).** The valley can now press its olives into oil, send goods by cart to a port that pays its own prices, and take a contract for oil that pays as it is delivered and costs a penalty if it is not kept. Every sum goes through the game's ledger, and tests show that no money can be made by carrying goods in a circle. The port's name is real; its prices, buyer and contract are invented and the game says so, with historical review pending. A game saved before this change is carried forward. Goods still arrive the day they are sent and prices do not yet move. In seven languages, machine-translated. The game remains a prototype on the test address only.
- **The Granada game has three picture settings, wind in its trees, and a first proof picture for the founder to judge (games workshop; not on the site).** Low, Medium and High can be chosen from the top bar; the game itself is the same at each. Trees and crops now move in the wind. A proof picture was taken from the running game and set beside the founder's target picture, with an honest account of each point he asked for: the layout of the target is there (an estate, a town, a walled palace on its hill, mountains), and its richness of detail is not. No more buildings will be made in number until he has judged it.
- **The games' music can now travel to where the games are published (test copy first; nothing public).** The museum's own suite plays in every game, but its sound files are deliberately kept out of the code repository, so the games published to the test copy were silent. The six tracks now have a route of their own: they are carried privately to the museum's storage, each one checked against a recorded fingerprint so that nothing but the museum's own music can be put there, and the games' server hands them to a player piece by piece, as browsers ask for audio. A game still makes no sound until you first click or press a key, and one switch turns the music off for all of them.

- **The museum's music joins the footer.** Every page's footer now carries a SoundCloud button beside the podcast buttons, linking to "Voices of the Museum", the museum's own six-track album (https://soundcloud.com/islam-museum/sets/voices-of-the-museum), so a visitor who reaches the bottom of any page can go straight to the music. The link lives in the central links module (`site/src/lib/links.ts`), and the button uses SoundCloud's glyph as an inline SVG like the other platform buttons; its accessible name is the platform and the album title, so no new text needed translating.
- **Hudhud: The Atlas of Wonders, a new story game, begins with one scene (games workshop, a prototype, not on the site, not released anywhere).** The founder gave a new 2D game sole priority among the museum's games on 26 November 2026 and paused the others, with everything of theirs kept. Its guide is Hudhud, an orange hoopoe; the player is a young Storykeeper; a storm has scattered the Atlas of Stories across ten worlds, and fifty of the museum's subjects each hold a page. What exists is the first scene, a few minutes long: Ibn al-Haytham's dark workshop, where you fly to five mirrors and turn them until a beam of evening light reaches a pale page, with a scholar to question, a cat to greet, a curtain that turns the room into a dark room with the town upside down on its wall, and a feather to find. You begin by choosing a girl or a boy explorer, whose skin, clothes and hair can be changed. It plays by keyboard, touch or entirely from a list in words, in the museum's seven languages, with three ways of playing and the museum's own music. Said plainly: the pictures are drawn by code an AI agent wrote and are not at the level of the founder's own pictures of Hudhud, which the game's page says and the founder is asked to judge; the six translations are machine drafts; the history is entered in the review ledger as pending and no reviewer is named; nobody but the author's script has played it; and it was measured on one machine only. With it: the founder's instruction filed unedited, a checked table of his 80 thumbnails as 50 subjects in ten worlds joined to museum records, the choice of a 2D engine (Phaser 4.2.1) with its measurements, a design, an art plan that sets out how real art could be made, and a plan (not built) for a Play page on the site. `docs/gaming/hudhud/`, `docs/gaming/games/hudhud.md`.
- **Hudhud keeps your place, lets you choose your keys, and can fill the screen (games workshop, a prototype, not on the site).** If you close the page in the middle of the light workshop, the mirrors you turned, what you found and the drawn curtain are there when you come back, behind a Continue button; a file the game cannot trust gives a fresh start, never a broken one. In Settings each action (left, right, fly, drop, touch) shows its keys and can be given another, and no key ever does two things. A Full screen button fills the screen where the browser allows it. A new browser check proves in real Chrome that the place is kept, that a changed key works, and that the whole scene can still be finished from the list in words on a device that cannot draw it.
- **Hudhud opens on the Atlas itself: ten worlds and fifty pages by name, one of them open (games workshop, a prototype, not on the site).** The game now begins on a page that names all ten worlds and the fifty people, places and stories in them, in seven languages, and says how many pages have come home. One quest, the light workshop, can be played from it; the other forty-nine are marked "Not built yet" and nothing pretends otherwise, and Sindbad and the Monkey and the Tortoise are marked as stories, not biographies. Finish a quest and you return to the Atlas with its page home. Three faults in saving that a review found are mended: changing save slot no longer wipes the other slot's place, the last mirror is kept if the page is closed while the scholar is still praising you, and an old tab can no longer put an older place back over a newer one.
- **Hudhud: the rules of a second kind of puzzle, and a plain list of what remains (games workshop, a prototype, not on the site).** For al-Jazari's elephant clock, which the museum's record describes as a ball passing from a falcon to a dragon to a vessel with a gong every half hour, the game now has tested rules for a machine as a row of parts, each handing its motion to the next: put them in the right order and the gong sounds; get one wrong and it stops there and shows where. These are rules only: no room is drawn for them and no quest uses them yet. Alongside, a page answers the founder's question of what stands between one scene and a whole game of many hours, item by item, including what only people can do (`docs/gaming/hudhud/remaining.md`).
- **Hudhud can be tried on the games' test address (UAT; a prototype, not on the site, not in production).** At the founder's word the games were released to the test host with Hudhud: The Atlas of Wonders as a fourth game beside Granada, The Golden Age and Atlas, whose own code did not change. It was then checked there in a real browser in all seven languages: the Atlas opens, the one quest plays to its end, the museum's music streams, and nothing is asked of any other server. The other three games passed their regression run on the same release. A new tool makes that check repeatable for any games host.
### Fixed
- **A pause at every change of season in The Golden Age is gone.** The game stopped for about a twentieth of a second each time a season ended. An earlier note blamed new buildings; timing each action showed it was the sky's lighting being swapped with the season. It now changes without the pause, and a whole scripted game ran with no slow frame.

### Data
- **Tranco, 25 November 2026: #608,280.** The museum's daily Tranco reading climbs 21,645 places in a day, from #629,925 on the list of 24 November to #608,280 on the list dated 25 November 2026 (list 947P2), read from the published full list of 4,326,585 domains before the API carried it. Forty-five days after opening, the museum stands 4,001,687 places above its first Tranco reading (#4,609,967 on the list of 23 October 2026). The ranking log in `docs/status.md`, the evidence in `site/src/data/traffic.json` and the traffic page carry the new figure.

## v2.30.0 — 2026-11-24
### Added
- **Palestine dossier prose, in seven languages.** First prose articles for the records created in the historic-buildings dossier merge (#8023): seven buildings — Tankiziyya and the Salahiyya madrasa in Jerusalem, the Great Mosque of Nablus (Jami' Nablus al-Kabir), the Great Mosque of Jenin (Fatima Khatun), al-Khadra Mosque in Nablus, the Omari Mosque of Dura and Qasr al-Basha in Gaza — plus the towns of Jenin and Dura. Each ships in Arabic, English, Urdu, French, Spanish, Turkish and Indonesian, cited to the dossier-registered sources.
- **The shelves wave: ten new class-driven browsers, in seven languages.** Ten new front doors over the one graph, each reading its membership from the records themselves (class, kind, roles, occupations and `<slug>-browser` tags) through the shared spec registry `scripts/shelves.ts` and the shared page `site/src/components/sig/ShelfPage.astro`: `/[lang]/imara/` (Sacred Architecture: every building that is not a tomb or shrine, by kind family), `/[lang]/collection/` (Objects and Artifacts by material), `/[lang]/tasawwuf/` (the Sufi orders, the mystics and their works), `/[lang]/kalam/` (Theology and Philosophy: sects, mutakallimun, falasifa), `/[lang]/nisa/` (Women of Islam: every woman on record by role family), `/[lang]/uhud/` (Covenants and Diplomacy: treaty events, charters, envoys), `/[lang]/maahid/` (Institutions of Learning: madrasas, libraries, observatories, bimaristans), `/[lang]/mawt/` (Tombs and Resting Places), `/[lang]/ulum/` (Sciences and Scientists by field) and `/[lang]/funun/` (Arts and Artists by art). Each ships its page in Arabic, English, Urdu, French, Spanish, Turkish and Indonesian, a progressive-enhancement filter, a whole-list filter index row, an Explore menu entry, `/api/v1/<slug>.json` (documented in the OpenAPI file and `llms.txt`), plan documents (77–86) and acceptance specs (70–79). Curated membership opens through `<slug>-browser` + `<slug>-<section>` tags; no record was moved or duplicated.

### Fixed
- **Page-weight budget for `/[lang]/sighar/storytellers/` raised to 200 KB.** The storytellers band hub measured 170.2 KB against the 170 KB band-hub ceiling in `check-weight.ts`, failing the build; the sibling explorers hub already sits at 280 KB, so the storytellers ceiling is raised to 200 KB to match the family.

Discord servers, forums and Reddit groups are deliberately not listed because they could not be opened and read. The new records and the new `vpdepth` interface text are in Arabic and English (and Urdu for the interface text); French, Spanish, Turkish and Indonesian fall back to English until the Word-translation round imports them.
- **A tenth arch with no door.** «I want it all: no filters, no doors» stands beside the nine doors of the landing page and leads straight to everything, at `/{lang}/browse/`, in all seven languages.
- **A treasure hunt: seven riddles and a final secret, at `/{lang}/hunt/` in all seven languages.** Seven places speak, from the cave of the first word to the library of Baghdad; naming each one opens the next. A hint leads to a museum page, the answer can always be shown, and progress stays on your own device: no account, nothing sent anywhere. It works without script, with every riddle open. The riddles are the record `exhibit/hunt-seven-places`; Arabic and English were written directly, the rest is machine translation not yet read by a person. Linked under the nine doors of the landing page; not rewrites-all-pages.
- **Viewpoints: nine ways in to the same museum, replacing the five persona doors of the landing page.** Under the Grand Tour button the landing page now asks «Which door are you coming in by?» and shows an arcade of nine doors, each with a different arch (New to Islam, Returning to Islam, Five years on, Curious, Doubting, Researching, Learning my faith, Challenging, Just passing through), each with a short name and a first-person line, opening on hover and keyboard focus. Each opens `/{lang}/for/<key>/`: its own accent, the thoughts you may have, a reading order of numbered steps with minutes linking to existing halls, and one specific block, in all seven languages (Arabic and English written by hand, the rest machine translation not yet read by a person). The old `/for/convert/`, `/for/doubter/`, `/for/researcher/`, `/for/learner/` and `/for/critic/` addresses still work and lead to the new pages. A small script (`/shell/viewpoint.js`) remembers your last viewpoint on your own device only; nothing is sent anywhere and the pages work without it. Changes the landing page and the `/for/` pages only; not rewrites-all-pages. Documented in `docs/site/viewpoints.md`.
- **A new hall: the Tajwid and Tilawah Browser («متصفح تجويد وتلاوة القرآن»), at `/{lang}/tajwid/` in all seven languages.** It opens on the makhraj map («خريطة مخارج الحروف»): the seventeen articulation points of the Jazariyya drawn in five regions — throat, tongue, lips, the empty mouth and the nose — with every letter set at its makhraj. Below it stand the Qur'an verses of the reviewed table in `scripts/tajwid.ts` (the measure of recitation, the etiquette of reciting and hearing, the recitation taught and heard), then the sections: the five corpora (Qur'an, Sunnah, seerah, tafsir, books) and the curated chapters (ahkam, adab, taalim, qurra, mutun, maqamat). Other passages join by a guarded lexicon over their wording at each build, so a book harvested later appears on its own; they are not reviewed one by one, and `TAJWID_EXCLUDE` is the escape hatch. The home page and the Explore menu carry the new entry. The dataset is at `/api/v1/tajwid.json`.
- **Two canonical mutun harvested into passages, from Arabic Wikisource.** Tuhfat al-Atfal of Sulayman al-Jamzuri (61 bayts, 8 chapter records) and al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya of Ibn al-Jazari (107 bayts, 16 chapter records) are filed as `unit: other` passage records with `ref` per chapter, the text copied verbatim from the Wikisource pages (CC BY-SA 4.0; the authors died after 1198 AH and in 833 AH), each with a provenance note in all seven languages, citing `source/ar-wikisource` and registered in `docs/library/harvest-register.yaml`.
- **Fourteen existing records join the browser by tag** (`tajwid-browser` plus `tajwid-<section>` and `tajwid-<topic>` tags): the concepts tajwid and tartil, the practices tajwid and sujud al-tilawa, the works al-Jazariyya, Tuhfat al-Atfal, al-Shatibiyya, al-Nashr and Tayyibat al-Nashr and Ghayat al-nihaya, and the persons Ibn al-Jazari, al-Shatibi, al-Dani, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and 'Ubada ibn al-Samit.
- **Plan and acceptance spec**: `docs/plan/76-tajwid-tilawah-browser.md` and `docs/engineering/68-tajwid-browser-requirements.md` (the founder's brief kept in his words, the requirements TJ-R1 to TJ-R15 and the production tests).
- **Season 3 of the children's podcasts joins both museum feeds.** `site/public/podcast/feed.xml` and `site/public/podcast/feed-ar.xml` now carry thirty episodes each: the ten new English stories of Hudhud's Story Time Season 3 (Ibn Khaldun, al-Razi, Wallada, al-Jahiz, Ibn Jubayr, Timbuktu, al-Khalil, Sindbad, Nur al-Din and al-Ghazali) and the ten new Arabic stories of «وقت حكايات هدهد» Season 3 (Ibn Firnas, al-Jazari, Ibn Battuta, Fatima al-Fihri, Ibn al-Nafis, al-Khwarizmi, Kalila wa Dimna, Ibn al-Haytham, al-Idrisi and al-Kindi), every item tagged with its iTunes season and episode numbers and carrying the link back to its museum record, as the earlier seasons do. - **Open Access Policy page and dated access audit, in the museum's seven languages.** A new standing page — *Open to Everyone: Humans and Machines* (`/{lang}/open-access/`) — states who may read and reuse the museum: people, search engines, AI training and agent crawlers, scrapers, archives and API clients, at any legitimate volume, with attribution encouraged but never a condition of reuse. Beside it, a dated transparency note (`/{lang}/open-access/audit/`) records the 24 November 2026 audit of the delivery configuration: all 33 named crawlers allowed, the browser-integrity filter switched off, and the robots.txt Content-Signal correction (PR #8189) recorded as pending the next deployment. Linked from the footer, the Why page, the licences page, the developers page and llms.txt.

Each file's front matter lists Microsoft Translator among its translators and the splice in its provenance. The translations are machine-made and unread by a human.
- **Eleven Urdu al-Tabari sections retranslated.** The first Urdu Word files returned these eleven records still in Arabic; a small retry document was translated and spliced in their place (16:96, 16:105, 20:38, 21:2, 21:54, 22:7, 22:43, 22:44, 23:40, 23:94, 27:77).
### Changed
- **264 more pages in French, Spanish, Turkish and Indonesian, translated by a language model (Claude) in the repo, not by Google or Word.** 37 French and 46 Spanish pages (from English) and 100 Turkish and 81 Indonesian pages (from Arabic) are new, each stamped with its provenance (model, run and source) and marked as machine translation not read by a human. Pages over 6,000 Arabic words (28 long works and passages) were left out. Where a source page carried leaked English or Urdu fragments, only its real text was translated.
- **About 1,400 more Turkish and about 580 more Indonesian prose pages, machine-translated from Arabic through Microsoft Word with the paragraph-per-fragment scheme.** The new pages are Word's machine translation and no human has read them; each carries its provenance and cites the same sources as its Arabic page. Records the importer refused (lost placeholders, changed emphasis marks, typed honorifics) and 16 files that failed the validator's perspectives or reading-level rules were left untranslated rather than loosening any check; the gap to Arabic is now about 300 pages in Turkish and about 80 in Indonesian.
- **robots.txt now welcomes AI training and AI input.** The Content-Signal line in `site/public/robots.txt` changes from `ai-train=no, search=yes, ai-input=no` to `ai-train=yes, search=yes, ai-input=yes`, so the museum's crawler policy matches its open licence (the data is CC0) and the founder's unrestricted-access policy: search engines, AI trainers and AI agents are all invited to read the museum.

### Fixed
- **The whole-site check survives a big sitemap.** `scripts/check-site.ts` joined every sitemap file into one string; past roughly half a gigabyte of URLs V8 refuses the string and the check crashed with "Invalid string length". It now searches each sitemap file separately.
### Fixed
- **The access-audit page builds.** `/<lang>/open-access/audit/` imported the site layout one directory level too shallow, so the Astro build failed at the entrypoint step; its imports now resolve one level deeper, like every other page nested three under `[lang]`.
### Fixed
- **One al-Suyuti report, one record.** The fragment filed on 15:43 is the second half of the report on 15:45; its address now leads to the 15:45 record, which holds the whole text and links both verses.
- **19 of al-Suyuti's reports moved to the verse they are about.** The 346 Lubab al-Nuqul records were checked against the Qur'an text and against the book's own verse order; 19 were filed under a verse that opens with the same words. Labels, references, links and prose now agree in all seven languages; the addresses are unchanged. The report on 15:45, cut in mid-sentence, is complete.
- **53 of al-Wahidi's reports moved to the verse they are about.** Each record's heading was matched against the Qur'an text in the repository; 53 were filed under another verse, sixteen of them under another sura (al-Hujurat and al-Hajj under al-Hijr, al-Anbiya under Ta-Ha). Labels, references, links and prose now agree in all seven languages; the addresses are unchanged.
- **Coverage totals regenerated from a fresh graph**, with the twelve new al-Wahidi records counted.
- **A mistranslated name corrected in Turkish and Indonesian.** Two Ahmed El-Sayed lectures speak of al-Hums, the name Quraysh used for themselves before Islam; the machine translation had turned it into the name of a modern organisation. The old Persian word for army in the Turkish page on Isfahan is spelled «Sipah». The content-safety check is clean again.
- **148 long occasion-of-revelation reports are whole again.** An earlier import cut reports of al-Suyuti and al-Wahidi at about 220 words; 43 and 105 of them now run to their end as in the OpenITI text, in all seven languages (about 23,500 Arabic words each). Twelve of al-Wahidi's that run on into the next verse's report are left as they were until they are divided.
- **The occasion-of-revelation reports read whole and in the right direction.** The 764 reports of al-Suyuti and al-Wahidi were compared with their OpenITI source. In the six non-Arabic languages the section headed as the full report held only a cut-off fragment on 697 of them; it now carries the same Arabic text as the Arabic page. 327 words glued together where an honorific had been removed are separated, and a few plain digitisation typos in the source (such as «الوحداي» for «الواحدي») are corrected. Any paragraph written wholly in Arabic inside another language's prose is now marked as Arabic and right-to-left, for screen readers and for layout, on every page that has one. Reports longer than about 220 words are still cut there, as on the Arabic pages.
- **Bookkeeping caught up.** The Ahmed El-Sayed ledger marks Reformers episodes 25 to 32 as merged, and `docs/coverage.md` counts the treasure hunt exhibit.
- **A machine-translation false cognate on verse 48:22.** Al-Tabari's phrase «ولن يُغْلَبَ حِزْبٌ اللَّهُ ناصِرُهُ» — the classical "party of God" — was rendered in English as the name of a modern organisation; it now reads "the party of God, whose helper He is, will never be defeated". The content-safety check is clean again.
- **Validation errors unblocking the build.** The altafsir.com text record of Jami' al-Bayan (`data/work/jami-al-bayan-altafsir-web.yaml`) now carries its `status` line; the open-access audit strings in the Arabic and Urdu interface files wrap their Arabic-script parentheses in isolates; and eleven translation files (verses 36:58, 44:24 and 88:23) no longer carry a stray `<sup>1</sup>` footnote tag that the Arabic original does not have.
- **Three Ahmed El-Sayed lecture records no longer generalise about a people.** In the Reformers Seerah, episodes 23, 24 and 28, wording about Jews in general now names the group the lecturer speaks of or is removed, two historical statements about Banu Qurayza are restored in neutral wording, and a report from Anas on the poisoned sheep that had been displaced in four languages is back. In all seven languages.

## v2.28.0 — 2026-11-23
### Added
- **Seven new person records for notable converts to Islam (converts section, wave 2): Maryam Jameelah, Murad Wilfried Hofmann, Martin Lings, Jeffrey Lang, Alexander Russell Webb, Nasreddine (Étienne) Dinet and Yahiya Emerick.** Each tells who the person was, the path to Islam as the cited sources report it, what they did afterwards, the difficulties and reactions, and criticism where the sources give it, in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish, with two or more independent sources read in full, the `convert` story role and the theme `converts-and-leavers`. Faith values are recorded only on their documented basis. Gary Miller was held because no independent source could be read (`docs/delegation/converts-wave2-held.md`).
- **A written proposal for a converts section, `docs/delegation/converts-proposal.md` (no content is added by it).** It records what the museum already holds on people who came to Islam (about 177 people carry the theme, 108 the role, nearly all early Muslims), lists about 60 famous converts to cover, proposes three exhibits (the famous converts by era, the first year, and five years on), written as what converts report and what named scholars say and never as instructions, and lays out the work in batches of up to 25 records with the source families to register first.
- **Local-model tooling for the Ahmed Elsayed podcast harvest, so extraction and translation can run on the founder's Mac without API cost.** `scripts/harvest/ahmed-el-sayed/local_extract.py` makes a claims file with a local model, keeping a claim only when the verbatim quote it carries is found in the transcript and linking records by exact multi-word labels; `local_translate.py` translates into Urdu, French and Spanish with TranslateGemma 27B (kept on the microSD, run in its own Ollama server); `run_local.py` runs both for every transcribed episode and repairs or drops any claim that breaks a rule before the usual checkers run. Records made this way say so in their provenance.
- **The rest of «السيرة النبوية للمصلحين» (The Prophetic Biography for Reformers) joins the museum: episodes 25 to 32, which completes the 32-episode series of Ahmed Elsayed.** Same form as the first 24: each lecture record says what he narrates and explains, attributed to him, in five languages, cited to the whole episode with no time and linked to existing records, with contested and polemical passages marked as his view. The episodes treat the harm done by the hypocrites, the treaty of Hudaybiyya, the expeditions of Dhu Qarad and Khaybar, the return of the emigrants from Abyssinia, the Umra of al-Qada and the battle of Mu'ta, the conquest of Mecca and, in the last session, Hunayn, Tabuk and the farewell pilgrimage. The series record now lists all 32 episodes.
- **A second lecture series of Ahmed Elsayed joins the museum: «السيرة النبوية للمصلحين» (The Prophetic Biography for Reformers), episodes 1 to 24 of 32, as one series record and 24 lecture records in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish.** The series, first published as audio between March and October 2023, follows the Prophet's life for those who work to reform: each episode record says what he narrates and explains, attributed to him, in about a dozen topic sections with links to the museum records they touch, and cites the whole episode with no time. Where he judges a person or a group, or states a religious position firmly (on the fate of Abu Talib, on the Shia view of the Companions, on whether faith may be blurred), the record is marked contested or polemical and says the view is his and not the museum's. Passages that generalised about a whole people were left out. The text was written by AI models from a Whisper transcript and checked mechanically; it has not been read by a human, and the Urdu, French and Spanish are AI translations from the English. Episodes 25 to 32 follow in the next batch.
- **The Cloudflare version-retention note now carries the live figures from the dashboard (23 November 2026).** It records 19,933 Pages deployments (about 3,500 older than 30 days), shows they come from Pages' own GitHub integration (previews of every branch plus a build of every push to `main`) and 36 site Worker versions (all kept), corrects the claim that the setup makes no Pages previews, and opens a question for the founder on whether to keep that integration.
- **An engineering note on Cloudflare's new version retention (from 8 December 2026), `docs/engineering/67-cloudflare-version-retention.md`.** It reads the repository's own Cloudflare setup (Pages, the site Worker, seven sync Workers, R2) against the change that deletes Worker and Pages versions older than 30 days and keeps the 100 newest: it finds that no URL, preview or R2 object depends on an old version, that Cloudflare rollback only covers code and not the content in R2, and that the working rollback is redeploying one of the five newest kept builds. It lists the docs that overstate Pages rollback, five questions only the live account can answer, and optional deploy-record habits that need the founder's approval. Nothing in the deploy setup was changed.
- **Five doors into five views of the museum, under the Grand Tour button on the landing page.** "Just converted", "Still deciding", "Researcher", "Learning my deen" and "Critic" (each a coloured button with an arrow) open `/{lang}/for/{persona}/`, a view of the same museum with its own colour, the thoughts such a visitor may have, a reading order and links into the existing halls. The convert view also lays out a path from the first days to the second year (first prayers, finding one person, telling family, food and drink, the first Ramadan, doubt and hardship, comparing with Christianity or Judaism, getting to know yourself). Written in all seven languages; the Urdu, French, Spanish, Turkish and Indonesian text is machine-translated and not yet read by a human. No script is needed. The museum still has no checked directories of halal shops, bookshops, support groups or forums, and the convert view says so. Design notes: `docs/site/personas.md`.

Every claim is the speaker's own account with a timestamp citation; the Banu Qurayza judgment and Abu Dharr's move to al-Rabadha — both contested — carry perspectives blocks with no verdict; garbled lines and the speaker's unchecked figures are marked needs_source. The sections were written by an AI agent and not verified by a human.


### Changed
- **Word translation files can now be built so the importer gets almost every record back (`--scheme frag`).** Word for Mac was dropping or garbling the citation and link placeholders inside lines, so most records were refused. The new scheme sends each piece of text as its own paragraph and puts citations and links back by position. On a test file, 23 of 25 Turkish records passed, against 5 of 226 before. Recorded in `docs/engineering/63-translation-by-document-files.md`; machine translation, not read by a human.

## v2.27.0 — 2026-11-21
### Added
- **Twenty-five lessons from the Mufti Ismail ibn Musa Menk YouTube channel, as records in seven languages (Arabic, English, Urdu, Spanish, French, Turkish, Indonesian).** Each record is a short lecture or sermon of the speaker's own, with a summary and a timestamped list of what he says, citing the video by its time (`content/<lang>/work/yt-*.md`, `data/work/yt-*.yaml`). The audio and transcripts stay out of git; the points are his own words in the museum's own, each cited to the minute.
