By their titles, they cover the effects of Umar's conversion, the economic and security boycott of the Prophet and the clans of Hashim and al-Muttalib, the lives of the early emigrants to Abyssinia, the lessons of the revelation of Surat Abasa, the objections the idolaters raised against the call, the later return of some Companions from Abyssinia, the ending of the boycott document, the journey to al-Ta'if and the protection of al-Mut'im, and the deaths of Khadija and Abu Talib with the Isra. The series record now lists all 32 episodes. - **The first lecture series of Ahmed Elsayed's podcast joins the museum: «سيرة رسول الله» 2026, episodes 1 to 24 of the 32 in the public feed, as one series record and 24 lecture records in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish.** Each episode record says what he narrates and explains in that lecture, attributed to him ("He says", "He holds"), in about a dozen topic sections, each followed by the museum records it touches (the Prophet's family and the Quraysh, the first revelation, the early Muslims, the boycott, the Hijra to Abyssinia, Ibn Hisham's Sira and its commentators and many more; between 37 and 115 links an episode, 1,518 in all). Every claim is cited to the whole episode with no time, for example `{cite:podcast-ahmed-el-sayed seerah-2026/ep7}`, and the citation links to the episode's SoundCloud page. Where he takes a side in a dispute, or speaks harshly of a group, the record is marked contested or polemical and says the view is his and not the museum's. His prayers, exhortations and comments on today's events are left out. The text was written by AI models from a Whisper transcript of the audio and checked mechanically; it has not been read by a human, speech recognition may have misheard names, and the Urdu, French and Spanish are AI translations from the English. The audio and transcripts are not published. Episode 28 is not in the public feed, and episodes 25 to 33 follow in the next batch.
- **A new harvest lane for Ahmed Elsayed's podcast «أحمد السيد», opened with its source, its ledger and its citation form (nothing is published on the site yet).** The podcast is registered as `source/podcast-ahmed-el-sayed`, a modern scholar's narration and so a secondary source, with its feed, posture and limits in `scripts/harvest/sources.yaml`, the harvest register, `docs/agents/source-families.md` and `docs/attribution.md`. The lane page `docs/agents/lanes/ahmed-el-sayed.md` fixes the citation rule: a citation names the narrator, the series, the episode number and links to the whole episode page, with no timestamp (`{cite:podcast-ahmed-el-sayed seerah-2026/ep33}`), and the site now resolves such a locator to the episode's SoundCloud page. The ledger `harvest/ahmed-el-sayed/ledger.tsv` lists the 835 episodes of the public feed read on 23 November 2026 in 47 groups, each with its upload date, duration and links; it records where the feed differs from the brief (835 episodes against about 1,400 expected; episode numbers missing in «سيرة رسول الله» 2026, «غيث الساري» and «أسئلة الجيل»). No audio was downloaded and no episode was transcribed. `scripts/ahmed-el-sayed-ledger.test.ts` keeps the ledger, the citation map and the locators in step.
- **A narrated walkthrough film of the Arabic Language Browser, in Arabic (marketing source only, nothing on the site changes).** `marketing/arabiyya-walkthrough/` holds the scripts and narration of a two-minute film for social media, in a landscape cut and a vertical cut for phones. It scrolls the live Arabic Language Browser: the ring of the letters in al-Khalil's order, the verses that name the tongue of the revelation, the nine chapters, the pages of the science of grammar and of Sibawayh down to their sources, and the passages found in the hadith, seerah and tafsir. It reuses the Place map film's voice, look and music. The README lists what each claim rests on; the founder's "ten doctorates and a hundred studies" is kept as a simile, not a count. The videos, footage and voice stay out of git.

- **Eight new records from pages 61 to 120 of the Arabic translation of Rashid al-Din's Jami' al-Tawarikh (volume 2, part 1): Ghiyath al-Din ibn Rashid, Ibrahim ibn Rashid al-Din, Narin Taghay, Izz al-Din Talib Dalqandi; the 717 dismissal and the 718 and 736 executions of the Rashid family and Ghiyath; and the 710 completion of the book, each giving the book's account, attributed to the book, with a note where no independent Sunni view is sourced.**
- **Seventeen new records from the first 60 scanned pages of the Arabic translation of Rashid al-Din's Jami' al-Tawarikh (volume 2, part 1: the Ilkhanid history): the book and Wassaf's history as sources; the men around Ghazan's court, including Sadr Jahan, Sa'd al-Din al-Sawaji, Ali Shah al-Jilani, Wassaf, Hafiz-i Abru and the Alid naqib Taj al-Din; the events of 697, 700, 702, 706 and 710 AH; the Rab' al-Rashidi quarter at Tabriz; and two open questions, on Rashid's birth year and on the claim of his Jewish origin, each giving the book's accounts side by side with a note where no Sunni view is sourced.**
- **A new hall: the Arabic Language Browser («متصفح اللغة العربية لغة القرآن»), at `/{lang}/arabiyya/` in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish.** It opens on the ring of the letters, the Arabic letters in the order al-Khalil ibn Ahmad gave them by place of articulation. Below it stand the fifteen verses in which the Qur'an speaks of its own tongue, nine chapters of records (Arabic as the language of the Qur'an, the inimitability of its language, origins and history, letters and script, the sciences of Arabic, dialects, Arabic in the world, the scholars, the books), and 77 passages from the hadith, the seerah, the tafsir and the other harvested books that speak about Arabic. The passages are found by their wording each time the site is built, so a book harvested later joins on its own; they are not reviewed one by one. The home page and the Explore menu carry the new entry. The dataset is at `/api/v1/arabiyya.json`.
- **22 new records with full prose in five languages**, among them: what four classical commentators say on why the Qur'an is Arabic; the men of Quraysh who heard it and what they said; the challenge verses and the books on inimitability (al-Rummani, al-Khattabi, al-Baqillani, al-Jurjani); the reports on learning Arabic with each one's grading; the debate on foreign words in the Qur'an; the origin of language; grammar, morphology and prosody; the dialects of the tribes and today's spoken Arabic; the Semitic family; the Arab countries; Arabic at the United Nations; and what Arabic gave other languages. Every judgement is given under the name of the scholar who made it. The prose and its translations were written by an AI model from the cited sources and have not been read by a human.

### Data and content: constitutional text and language shares on the 22 "Arabic in ..." pages (21 November 2026)

- **Constitutional text section on all 22 country pages (Arabic, English, Urdu, French, Spanish).** Each page now gives the constitutional document, the article and the Arabic wording as a short cited quotation, with the museum's own translation into the page's language. The wording and the official addresses come from a research summary supplied to the museum, which the founder approved using without re-checking on 21 November 2026; the museum did not open the pages the summary names, and every page and source record says so. Where the summary says no official Arabic text is published (Comoros, Somalia) the original French or Somali wording is quoted.
- **Corrections to earlier statements.** Saudi Arabia: the earlier page said no clause names a language; the summary gives Article 1 in Arabic as naming Arabic as the Kingdom's language (only that clause is quoted), and the page now states that the two readings disagree and have not been reconciled. Syria: the 13 March 2025 Constitutional Declaration, Article 4, replaces the 2012 text as the operative reference, which stays cited as an earlier text. Sudan: Article 6(b), added in February 2025, makes Arabic and English the official languages for the work of government and calls Arabic the most widespread national language; it replaces the earlier note that an encyclopedia footnote was unclear. Libya (2011 Declaration, Article 1), Iraq (Article 4, with Turkmen and Syriac in the administrative units where their speakers are dense), Palestine (Basic Law, Article 4, paragraph 3, beside the earlier citation), Somalia (Article 5, Somali official, Arabic the second language), Djibouti (Article 1 co-official Arabic and French, Article 93 French text authoritative) and Comoros (Article 9, French original only) are added with their own notes.
- **Language shares section on all 22 pages.** Each page now gives the figure the research summary lists, with what is measured, the issuing body and the year, or the sentence "No official figure" with the reason the summary gives. Figures: Djibouti (INSTAD RGPH-3, 2024: Somali 78.4, French 41.6, Arabic 26.6, Afar 25.8, multiple responses; its Arabic figure combines French and Arabic 21.6 with Arabic only 5.1), Morocco (HCP 2024, non-exclusive, and the 2014 split of Amazigh), Tunisia (INS 2024, languages read and written among the literate aged 10 and over), Iraq (Ministry of Education to UNESCO, 2020, Arabic about 85, Kurdish about 21, other 3, which sum to 109 percent in the source, and the page says so) and Algeria (no official figure; a UNESCO GEMR paper cites 20 to 30 percent Tamazight as its author's estimate). Comoros and Mauritania are given only as raw unweighted microdata cases, with the warning, quoted from the summary, that the catalog pages themselves say such counts are not official population statistics.
- **Djibouti address unverified.** The summary gives the INSTAD report through a google.com search link; the underlying address is recorded exactly as it appears inside that link (with doubly encoded characters) and the source record says the museum has not verified that it works.
- **New source records (59).** One record per official document or address for the constitutional wording, and one per address for the language shares, each with the note "wording supplied in a research file, page not opened by the museum". The pages' "what this page has not reached" sections gain a dated note that the "not read" statements describe the museum's own earlier reading and were left as written.

It sets side by side how the Library of Congress (ISO 639-2: one language, ara), ISO 639-3 (macrolanguage ara with 28 active individual languages, two deprecated codes) and Ethnologue 29th edition 2026 (each variety its own language; 33 in its Arabic subgroup) classify Arabic, with a list of the varieties and their codes, and prefers none. Judeo-Arabic varieties sit under jrb, Hassaniyya and Maltese are outside ara in Ethnologue, Juba Arabic is a creole. Source: a research summary supplied by the founder, used with his approval of 21 Nov 2026 without the museum opening the pages; no speaker numbers are given because Ethnologue withholds them. Linked to the Standard Arabic and dialects page, the tribal-dialects page and the six regional dialect pages. Tagged arabiyya-browser, arabiyya-dialects.

### Data
- Arabic language browser: five records of the Arabic language academies, each with full prose in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish, tagged arabiyya-browser and arabiyya-scholars: the Arab Academy of Damascus (origin 1918-1919, Muhammad Kurd Ali president 1919-1953), the Academy of the Arabic Language in Cairo (decree 31 December 1932, inaugurated 30 January 1934), the Iraqi Academy of Sciences (1947, with Kurdish and Syriac departments since 1963), the Jordan Academy of Arabic (first 1923-1924, re-established 1 July 1976) and the Union of Arab Language Academies (13 March 1971). Each links the persons and works the museum already holds (Kurd Ali, Taha Hussein, al-Jawari, Fuad I, Ahmad Rida, Matn al-Lugha, al-Mu'jam al-Wasit, al-Mu'jam al-Kabir) and says what its sources leave unknown (journal names, exact founding days, later history). Why it matters: readers of the browser can now see who made the modern terminology and Arabisation institutions of Arabic, in their own five languages.
- New concept concept/yawm-al-lugha-al-arabiyya-al-alami (World Arabic Language Day), tagged arabiyya-browser and arabiyya-world, in five languages: the 2010 United Nations decision to give a day to each of its six official languages, the choice of 18 December for Resolution 3190 (XXVIII) of 18 December 1973, and the observance since 2012. It links, and does not repeat, the existing speaker-figures page.
- Twelve new source records (English and Arabic Wikipedia, Encyclopedia.com and the official websites of the Cairo academy, the Jordan academy and the Union). All facts come from a research summary supplied to the museum; the pages were not opened by the museum, with the founder's approval of 21 November 2026, and each record says so. ### Data (arabiyya-browser, script)

Each states its date and calendar, find-place and present home, language and script, what it says (a paraphrase), and why it matters for the history of Arabic, and keeps the alternative dates and readings the research summary gives.

### Data
- Arabic language browser, poetry and philology (tag arabiyya-scholars): three new concept records, each a full article in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish: the Mu'allaqat (the seven odes and the three poets added in ten-ode recensions, with tribes and approximate dates), pre-Islamic poetry as linguistic evidence (the Masa'il of Nafi ibn al-Azraq to Ibn Abbas, and Sibawayh's verse citations in al-Kitab with Baalbaki's counts, attributed), and the schools of Basra and Kufa on witnesses, transmission and analogy (with Ibn al-Anbari's 121 points of dispute). Why it matters: readers of the browser can see how verse became the evidence on which Arabic grammar was built.
- Arabic proverbs (tag arabiyya-lisan): a concept on the great proverb books (Abu Ubayd, al-Askari, al-Zamakhshari, al-Maydani, with dates and counts) and ten short articles, one per well-known proverb, each with its story as the books tell it, its classical sources, its meaning and its use; each says the stories are legends as reported, not confirmed history. Slugs begin mathal-.
- Arabic literature (tags arabiyya-scholars, arabiyya-lisan): the eight periods of Arabic literature, the beginnings of the Arabic novel (Haykal's Zaynab, 1913), Naguib Mahfouz and the 1988 Nobel Prize, and language reform in the Nahda (al-Shidyaq, the two al-Yazijis, al-Bustani).
- Translation and Arabisation (tag arabiyya-world): the Abbasid translation movement and how Arabic became the language of science, nine Arabic scientific words in European languages (algebra, algorithm, alchemy, alcohol, zenith, nadir, azimuth, syrup, elixir), and Arabisation of the sciences with the language academies; it states both dates given for the ALECSO coordination bureau (1962 in this summary, 1961 in another).
- 86 new source records for every page the research summaries list (encyclopaedias, dictionaries, journals, library pages, commercial and learning sites alike). All facts come from research summaries supplied to the museum; the pages were not opened by the museum, with the founder's approval of 21 November 2026, and each record says so. Wikipedia pages support entity facts only.

### Data
- Arabic language browser: 23 new full-article records, each in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish (Arabic body 450+ words each), written from five research files supplied to the museum (pages not opened, founder approval 21 Nov 2026). Script and print (tag arabiyya-script): history of Arabic printing (1486 to the Beirut Imprimerie Catholique), printing, type and the Unicode Arabic block, the Arabic keyboard (ASMO 663, Arabic 101/102, Mac), the eleven languages written in the Arabic script (table of added letters, kept or replaced), the letters added in Persian and other languages, and Arabizi. Names (arabiyya-scholars): onomastics overview with the Ibn Khallikan example and an open proposal on structured name fields (awaiting the founder, schema unchanged), ism and kunya, nasab and nisba, laqab and khitab, elements of names (Abd, Ibn, Abu, Umm, al-, Al), how family names developed, and the reference works and authority files. Laws (arabiyya-world): Algeria's 1991 Arabisation law, Morocco's 2011 constitution, 2019 framework law 51-17 and organic law 26-16, Qatar's Law 7 of 2019, the UAE draft law (no enacted text found), and the Arab League, ALECSO and UNESCO. Institutions (group): King Salman Global Academy (2020), Arabic Language Academy in Sharjah (2016), the Arabic Language Centre in Dubai (1980, a private teaching institute), ALECSO and its Rabat Coordination Bureau (1961 here, 1962 in another file, both stated), and the Doha Historical Dictionary project (2013). Why it matters: readers of the browser can follow how Arabic was printed, encoded, typed and written by other languages, how its names work, and how states and organisations protect and plan it.
- 75 new source records for every page the research files list (each states: pages not opened, founder approval 21 Nov 2026).

### Added
- Ten new records for the Arabic Language Browser in all five languages, each a full article: how the four Sunni schools treat reciting the Qur'an in translation in prayer, the Friday sermon in a language other than Arabic, whether a translation counts as the Qur'an, and the duty to learn Arabic for worship (positions only, attributed to the named works, no ruling); the first Qur'an translations, translations by language with translators and dates, and why a translation is called an interpretation (al-Zarqani, al-Shatibi, Ibn Taymiyya, Pickthall); and, from the classical commentaries, what "clear Arabic tongue" means, the dispute over non-Arabic words, and whether inimitability lies in the text or in sarfa (al-Nazzam). They matter because readers can see each school's or author's view under its holder, with the work it comes from, and no verdict.
- 50 source records: one for every page the research summaries list (48) plus the two research summaries themselves; each says the pages were not opened and page numbers are unchecked.
### Changed
- The ten qira'at, the seven ahruf, Ibn Mujahid's selection of the seven, and the conditions of a sound reading gained sections: the ten readers with their narrators, death dates and features, the dialects linked to the seven ahruf with the other views, and the main works; they now also carry the arabiyya-browser and arabiyya-ijaz tags.

### Added (structured names on person records)

- **A person record can now carry its classical Arabic name as structured data (`name_parts`).** The founder approved the proposal on 21 November 2026. Each element of the name (given name, kunya, line of descent, epithet, honorific title, nisba, ancestral designation, the name the person is known by, spellings and source-attributed variants) can hold several values, each with its own sources, a certainty (attested, disputed or uncertain) and, for a nisba, an optional link to a place, tribe, occupation, dynasty or school that does not claim birth there or descent from it. The field is optional and no record is invalid without it. The validator checks that every cited source and linked record exists. Ibn Khaldun is the first record to use it. The shape is described in `docs/data/name-parts.md`. The site does not show it yet.

### Tests

- `scripts/name-parts.test.ts` checks the schema for the new field: the Ibn Khaldun record passes, several values and a link pass, and an unknown element, an unknown certainty, a malformed link and a missing value fail.

### Added (name card)

- **A person's page now shows a name card when the record carries structured name parts.** The card lists the classical Arabic name element by element (given name, kunya, descent, epithet, honorific title, affiliation, ancestral name), each with its transliteration, gloss, a "disputed" or "uncertain" mark where the sources are not sure, and, for an affiliation linked to a place, tribe, occupation, dynasty or school, a link to that record. A sentence under the card says a link shows an association only and never that the person was born there or descended from it. The card is plain HTML and ships in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish. Only pages of people whose records have `name_parts` change (Ibn Khaldun today), so the deploy stays small.

- Enriched ten Palestinian historic buildings from the founder-supplied palestine-buildings dossier (22 Nov 2026): al-Aqsa Mosque, Dome of the Rock, the Tankiziyya and Salahiyya madrasas, the Ibrahimi sanctuary, the Great Mosque of Nablus, the Great Mosque of Jenin (Fatima Khatun), al-Khadra Mosque, the Omari Mosque of Dura and Qasr al-Basha, Gaza — gaining foundation dates (EDTF + Hijri where the inscription gives it), patrons, UNESCO/ArchNet identifiers, locations, `located_in` relations and fuller seven-language summaries, each fact cited. Registered 22 new source records (UNESCO WHC and Tentative List pages, IRCICA inventory, MWNF, ArchNet companions, RIWAQ, Lemaire 1986, Pruitt 2017, Marom 2023, Aldohdar 2020, Taawon, Travel Palestine, Dura Municipality, WAFA, CNRS Gaza inventory, WMF Watch 2025, MEOC, Islamic Awareness, Aal al-Bayt white paper). Added two new place records, `place/jenin` and `place/dura`, in seven languages.
- Validation is clean again on main: the 25 `work/yt-*` Mufti Menk sermon records gained `delivered.by`, numeric durations, hyphenated slugs (renamed across data and all seven content languages) and had typed honorifics removed; `work/asbab-al-nuzul-wahidi` gained the alias `work/asbab-nuzul-wahidi` so ~2,500 Qur'an passage links resolve; `source/asbab-nuzul-wahidi-shamela-11314` field `url` corrected to `URL`.

### Changed
- **Rule change for one lane: audio of the YouTube channel @muftimenkofficial may be downloaded for local transcription (founder ruling, 21 November 2026).** The ruling is recorded in the sources policy and in the three documents that used to forbid YouTube downloads (plan 25, the audio and video harvest method, plan 15), scoped to that channel alone. The audio and transcripts stay in the harvest workspace and are never published; the museum publishes only its own wording, cited by timestamp, with a link to the video.

- **The YouTube lecture harvest can run its claims pass without the judge step, and the judge can follow later.** The harvest script gains two options: one produces claims and headers and holds each video at `claims_done`; the other runs the judge on videos already at that point. A claim is not counted as checked until the judge has run, so nothing moves to a record on the first pass. No site content changed.

### Added
- Muhammad Abduh's Risalat al-Tawhid, the treatise on the science of Tawhid, now has three concept entries in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish, drawn from the body of the book: good and ugly acts, God's knowledge and human choice (with the author's view labelled as his), and the general mission of the messengers and the miracle. The source and work records now say that the introduction and the body pages at scan pages 63 to 70 and 82 to 84 have been read; the rest of the book is not yet mined.
- How to Savour Prayer (Kayfa tatalaththadhu bi-al-salat), a video lecture series by Mishari al-Kharraz held in the Assabile archive, now has an entry in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish. It is written from the first three episodes of the machine transcript and covers presence of heart, understanding, hope and awe in prayer. The speaker's own figures and reports are marked as his and as needing a source, and passages the transcript renders unclearly are flagged rather than guessed.
- Wa Nalqa al-Ahibba, Amr Khaled (lecture series, Assabile archive): episodes 53 and 54 added in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish as drafts. Episode 53 covers the wars against the apostates after the Prophet's death, the claimants to prophecy (Tulayha, Sajah, Musaylima), the eleven armies Abu Bakr sent out, Khalid's campaign against Tulayha, the return of Tulayha and the capture of Uyayna ibn Hisn, and the killing of Malik ibn Nuwayra as the speaker tells it. Episode 54 covers the battle of Yamama against Musaylima: the Hanifa army, the death of Habib ibn Zayd, the tribal ranks, Abu Dujana and Zayd ibn al-Khattab, the walled garden, the peace with Mujjaa, and Khalid's later marriage. Every point is the speaker's account, with timestamps; the speaker's figures are marked as unchecked; the conflicts inside the transcript and with the record are stated; garbled and present-day passages are left out.
- Wa Nalqa al-Ahibba, Amr Khaled (lecture series, Assabile archive): episodes 49, 51 and 52 added in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish as drafts. Episode 49 is Tufayl ibn Amr al-Dawsi (his conversion on hearing a passage of the Qur'an, the light between his eyes, the conversion of his people Daws, the Prophet's prayer for them, and his death as a martyr at Yamama). Episodes 51 and 52 continue the Khalid ibn al-Walid series: his conversion on the road to Medina, Mu'tah and the withdrawal, the conquest of Mecca, Hunayn, Tabuk and Dumat al-Jandal, and Banu al-Harith. Every point is the speaker's account, with timestamps; figures and ages are marked as unchecked; the conflicts between the transcript and the record are stated; garbled passages and present-day framings are left out.
- Wa Nalqa al-Ahibba, Amr Khaled (lecture series, Assabile archive): episodes 45 and 46 added in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish as drafts. Episode 45 is Jabir ibn Abdullah (the second pledge of al-Aqaba, the lot for Uhud, his father's debts and death, the flood that uncovered the grave, the army fed from a handful of barley, and the camel sold to the Prophet). Episode 46 is Sumayya, Yasir and Ammar ibn Yasir (the first family to embrace Islam openly, Sumayya as the first martyr, Ammar's torment, Badr, and Umm Umara at Uhud and against Musaylima). Every point is the speaker's account, with timestamps; the figures and ages are marked as unchecked, the contested war account is framed as the speaker's, and the garbled passages are left out.
- Wa Nalqa al-Ahibba, Amr Khaled (lecture series, Assabile archive): episodes 36, 37 and 38 added in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish drafts. Episode 36 is Abu Ayyub al-Ansari (the Pledge of Aqaba, the Prophet's seven months in his house, the manners of visiting and asking permission, and his last campaign at Constantinople). Episode 37 is Abu Hurayra (his name, his years with the Prophet, the People of the Suffa, his memory of hadith as the speaker presents it, his mother's conversion and his worship). Episode 38 is Bilal ibn Rabah (his torture and purchase, the call to prayer, Badr and the conquest of Mecca, his last years in Damascus). Each statement is cited to the recording by timestamp; the speaker's dates, figures and reports are marked as needing a source. Machine transcripts, not listened to.
- **The children's podcasts now have their full record in the repository.** A new engineering document (65 · Podcast pipeline) sets out how "Hudhud's Story Time" (English) and «وقت حكايات هدهد» (Arabic) are made: the ElevenLabs voices, and why Arabic needed a grandfather voice of its own; scripts drawn only from the museum's own records; the picture-book videos; the pre-publish gate every episode must pass — a transcription checked line by line against the script, a loop scan, language checks down to five-second windows, a glyph preflight, and a page-by-page inspection — and the four defects that gate caught and fixed, among them a line one Arabic episode spoke in English. A companion outreach document (`docs/outreach/podcast-series.md`) catalogues all twenty episodes with the museum record each story came from and its YouTube link, records where the series stand (both complete on YouTube on 20 November 2026; the museum's own podcast feed goes live at the next deployment, with Apple Podcasts and Spotify to follow), and fixes the one sentence outreach may use about them.
- **The sack of Baghdad in 1258 now says what the TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi says about it, in Arabic, English and Urdu.** The event page gains a section with the encyclopaedia's accounts: Hulagu's march from Hamadan on 9 Rabīʿ I 655 (27 March 1257); the figures for the dead (800,000 to 2,300,000) and the differing reports on the caliph's killing and on Ibn al-ʿAlqamī; the books thrown into the Tigris and the river that ran for days the colour of ink, which the article on al-Mustaʿṣim presents as a report found in the sources; the caliph's own library, Khizānat al-Mustaʿṣim; and the date of the caliph's death, 20 Muḥarram 656 (27 January 1258), against the 10 Ṣafar of the programme account already on the page. The House of Wisdom page gains a section on its end: the encyclopaedia says Hulagu burned and destroyed it in 1258 after more than five hundred years. The page also lists its other names (Siege, Sack and Fall of Baghdad, 1258) so that a search finds it. Four encyclopaedia articles are new source records, and the encyclopaedia's own judgment that Islamic civilisation began to decline from this date is stated as its judgment only.
- Wa Nalqa al-Ahibba, Amr Khaled (lecture series, Assabile archive): episode 29 added, the third Aisha bint Abi Bakr episode, in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish drafts — the recap of the outings and the night prayer; the speaker's remarks on the privacy of the Prophet's household and the shared bathing vessel; the long women's-husbands hadith with the Abu Zar' and Umm Zar' story; the knot-in-the-rope exchange and the answer on why love lasts; the household's poverty and the wives' request for more maintenance that led to the verses of the choice, with Aisha's answer; the Prophet's last days (the nights, the nursing in her house), the siwak, the head on her chest, the angel-of-death report and the announcement of the death with Abu Bakr's words; her forty-odd years afterwards on the speaker's count, the first school, the tayammum occasion, the saying of Abu Musa and the nephew's question about medicine, the saying about eloquence, her night weeping over one verse, the Arafa fast, the perfumed coins; the studio participants' comments on marriage and on women's place; her part at Uhud and the Trench on his telling; her giving up the burial place to Umar, her wish to be buried with the other wives, and her death as he gives it with Ibn Abbas's glad tidings and the funeral; and the announcement that the ifk affair is kept for a separate episode and that Hafsa bint Umar comes next; each statement cited to the recording by timestamp, the contested material (the argument for the young bride, the ranking among narrators, the ninety-percent claim, the prayer-interruption question, the participants' opinions, the address to girls, love as mission, what her scholarship shows) kept under perspectives and attributed to the speaker or the participants, the museum's readings of garbled names and every unchecked figure listed in the 'left out' sections, one contemporary political example omitted; machine transcript, not listened to.
- Wa Nalqa al-Ahibba, Amr Khaled (lecture series, Assabile archive): episodes 30 and 31 added in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish drafts. Episode 30 is the slander affair (hadith al-ifk) as the speaker tells it: the return from Bani al-Mustaliq, the lost necklace, the rumour, the consultations, the revelation and the lessons, each statement cited to the recording by timestamp; the Qur'anic verses are linked, not typed. Episode 31 is Hafsa bint Umar: her family and marriages, her widowhood, Umar's search for a husband for her, the Prophet's marriage to her, the honey episode, the withdrawal from the wives and her death. Dates and ages are the speaker's, marked as needing a source; the contested material is kept under perspectives with no verdict. Machine transcripts, not listened to.
- Wa Nalqa al-Ahibba, Amr Khaled (lecture series, Assabile archive): episodes 39, 40 and 41 added in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish as drafts. Episode 39 is Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman (his choice of the Ansar, Badr and Uhud, his father, the night mission to the enemy camp at the Trench, the names of the hypocrites, and his governorship and death). Episode 40 is Sa'd ibn Mu'adh (the Throne shaking at his death, his conversion through Mus'ab ibn Umayr, Badr and the Trench, the judgement on Banu Qurayza as the speaker gives it, and his death). Episode 41 is Suhayl ibn Amr (his son Abd Allah, Badr, the treaty of Hudaybiyya and its clauses, the Conquest of Mecca, and his conversion and death). Every point is the speaker's account, with timestamps; the figures and the disputed judgement are marked as unchecked.
- Wa Nalqa al-Ahibba, Amr Khaled (lecture series, Assabile archive): episodes 42, 43 and 44 added in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish as drafts. Episode 42 is Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib (the uncle who lived to see the Prophet's death, the second pledge of al-Aqaba, Badr and the captives, the Conquest of Mecca and the Abu Sufyan episode, Hunayn, his prayer, and his death). Episode 43 is Ja'far ibn Abi Talib (the first emigration to Abyssinia, his five-point account before the Negus, the recitation of the opening of Surat Maryam, his return, and his martyrdom at Mu'ta). Episode 44 is Asma bint Abi Bakr (the Hijra and the carrying of food to the cave, Abu Jahl's visit, her generosity, her counsel to her mother, and her son Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr). Every point is the speaker's account, with timestamps; the figures, the ages and the disputed readings are marked as unchecked, and the garbled passages are left out.
- Wa Nalqa al-Ahibba, Amr Khaled (lecture series, Assabile archive): episodes 57, 58 and 59 added in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish as drafts. Episode 57 covers Khalid ibn al-Walid's march to Syria, the four armies, the desert crossing and the spring, the battle of Yarmuk and the single command, Umar's removal of Khalid, the entry into Damascus and Khalid's death. Episodes 58 and 59 cover the martyrs of Uhud, in two groups, as the speaker tells them. Every point is the speaker's account, with timestamps; the speaker's figures are marked as unchecked; the conflicts inside the transcripts are stated and not decided; garbled and present-day passages are left out.
- How to Savour Prayer (Kayfa tatalaththadhu bi-al-salat), a video lecture series by Mishari al-Kharraz held in the Assabile archive, now covers episodes 4 to 6 as well, in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish. Episode 4 is on love of God, His beauty and the sweetness of the love that accompanies fear and hope; episode 5 on God's good treatment of His servants and the shame of forgetting it; episode 6 on the blessing of favours and of inner and outer security, and on shame before God. Every point is the speaker's own account, attributed to him, with timestamps; his figures and his medical and factual claims are marked as needing a source, reports without a named chain are flagged, and passages the transcript renders unclearly are flagged rather than guessed. Passages outside the subject of the series are left out.
- How to Savour Prayer (Kayfa tatalaththadhu bi-al-salat), a video lecture series by Mishari al-Kharraz held in the Assabile archive, now covers episodes 7 to 9 as well, in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish. Episode 7 is on distraction in prayer, the reward that follows humility, and the speaker's 'magic key' of speaking to God in prayer; episode 8 on the call to prayer and what follows it; episode 9 on five kinds of people in prayer and on the congregation. Every point is the speaker's own account, attributed to him, with timestamps; his figures and his claims are marked as needing a source, reports without a named chain are flagged, and passages the transcript renders unclearly are flagged rather than guessed. Verses he cites without a verse number are not written out, and no passage link is added.
- How to Savour Prayer (Kayfa tatalaththadhu bi-al-salat), a video lecture series by Mishari al-Kharraz held in the Assabile archive, now covers episodes 10 to 12 as well, in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish. Episode 10 is on ablution: its intention and reward, the doubts that trouble some worshippers, and the speaker's account of how the Prophet performed it. Episode 11 is on the sins that the speaker says ablution removes and on the siwak. Episode 12 is on covering the awrah, adornment for God and preparing for the opening takbir. Every point is the speaker's own account, attributed to him, with timestamps; his statistics and claims are marked as needing a source; reports without a named chain are flagged; passages the transcript renders unclearly are flagged rather than guessed. Legal rulings on points where the schools differ are not written, and are listed for the founder. Verses he cites without a verse number are not written out, and no passage link is added.

### Added
- **The last four dictionaries of the research list are in the Dictionaries Browser: the Sharjah Historical Dictionary, the Cairo Academy's *al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr*, *Muʿjam matn al-lugha* and the Dictionary of the Contemporary Arabic Language.** Each is described and linked, not hosted. The Sharjah record is built from the project's own pages, read on 20 November 2026: it spans five eras from pre-Islamic inscriptions to modern use, is arranged by roots, and its statistics page then showed 12,009 roots, 78,259 words and 410,062 historical attestations (the home page of the same site showed smaller figures, which the record notes); its rights are reserved by the Arabic Language Academy in Sharjah. *Matn al-lugha* (Ahmad Rida, 5 volumes, 1958–1959) and Ahmad Mukhtar Umar's dictionary (4 volumes, 2008 edition of 3,367 pages) come from Wikidata with the revisions recorded, and each author has a record with dates. *al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr* rests on the TDV account of the Academy's plan and its 500-page specimen volume of 1956. The Doha and Sharjah records show that the research list's earlier claim of "127 volumes" for Sharjah is not what the project's own site states. The two namesakes called Aḥmad Riḍā are listed so that the validator keeps them apart.
### Added
- **Lane's Lexicon and the Doha Historical Dictionary are in the Dictionaries Browser, described and linked, not copied.** *An Arabic-English Lexicon* has a record with its author, Edward William Lane (17 September 1801 – 10 August 1876, from Wikidata with its revision recorded): eight parts, an 1863 edition by William and Norgate, recorded as public domain, running only to the letter qāf with later roots present but not complete, and where it can be read (Perseus, the Tyndale archive, an Internet Archive text version whose rights are not stated). The Doha Historical Dictionary has a record built from its own terms of use, quoted, which allow reuse only for personal non-commercial purposes, forbid derivative works without written permission and forbid commercial or AI-training use without permission, and from Arabica's note that Ramzi Baalbaki heads its Scientific Council; its own about and statistics pages load by script and could not be read, so the record says no more than that. The browser gains a section for historical dictionaries.
### Added
- **Ramzi Baalbaki's overview of the classical Arabic dictionaries, from Arabica, is now in the records.** Three more Arabica entries were read and registered (the overview, the entry on the word *muʿjam*, and the entry on al-Bakrī). From the overview: al-Jawharī (d. about 400 AH / 1010) was the first to make the alphabetical order of the root letters the only criterion of the rhyme system, probably following his uncle Isḥāq al-Fārābī, with al-Bandanījī (d. 284/897) before them considering only the last letter; *Lisān al-ʿArab*'s five sources and Ibn Manẓūr's reasons for them (collection and arrangement); that *al-Qāmūs* has about three times the proper names of *Lisān* and twenty times those of *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*; that *Tāj al-ʿArūs* took fourteen years to dictate, ended in 1188/1774, and has 11,978 roots against 9,273 and 5,618; and short notes on *Asās*, *Maqāyīs*, *Jamhara*, *al-Mukhaṣṣaṣ* and *Dīwān al-adab*. The earlier *Ṣiḥāḥ* sentence, which stated only that al-Bandanījī came first, is replaced by this fuller account. The browser's home gains a short note on what *muʿjam* and *qāmūs* originally meant: *muʿjam* meant a dotted book and was first used as a book title by the hadith scholars, and *qāmūs* meant "the ocean".
### Added
- **Ten more sources for the dictionaries, opened and checked: seven Arabica entries, two library catalogue records and one manuscript catalogue page.** Arabica, the Doha Institute's Arabic encyclopaedia, supplies scholarly profiles by named specialists; the National Library of Tunisia's catalogue gives the Bulaq printings of *Lisān al-ʿArab* (1883–1889, 20 parts in 10 volumes) and *al-Qāmūs* (1856, 2 volumes); the al-Raqq al-Manshur catalogue lists 302 manuscripts of *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*. New in the records: *Kitāb al-ʿAyn* now states Baalbaki's view that its plan is al-Khalīl's by near consensus while his share in the body is unresolved, and the debate on Indian or Greek influence with the voices of Lowe and Haywood, each attributed; *al-Jamhara* notes that Ibn Durayd's stated aim does not match its contents; *Maqāyīs* notes the disputed order with *Mujmal*; *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* notes the claim that al-Bandaniji's *al-Taqfiya* preceded al-Jawharī in rhyme order. Two further sources (HathiTrust, Iranica) refused an automated reader and were not used.
### Added
- **Entry starts are marked on the pages of al-Ṣiḥāḥ (1,214 pages so far), and the roots can be browsed.** A model read the machine text of each page and marked where each entry begins and its root; a script then checked every mark against the exact text, and nothing in the text was changed. Each marked page now shows one paragraph per entry with its root, and `/{lang}/maajim/sihah/roots/` lists the marked roots by first letter with links to the entries (6,382 entries so far). Of 6,607 marks, 95% matched the text exactly and 88 more matched on a shorter start; 225 (3.4%) were dropped because the start was too short or not found, and 14 pages carry no marks. The marks were checked against the page images by eye on three pages (pages 43 and 60 of volume 1, page 300 of volume 2): every entry on them was marked, with one root misread among them. A root can still be misread; the entry on the page is the evidence. The marked pages and roots are also in `/api/v1/maajim-sihah.json`.
### Added
- **The Dictionaries Browser lane has a progress file and a written list of which sources it trusts.** `docs/delegation/maajim-progress.md` records what is built and what is not, the five tests a source must pass before it carries a claim, and a four-tier sort of the 680 sources Gemini cited: those already opened and used (the TDV encyclopaedia, archive.org metadata), those to open and check before first use (manuscript and library catalogues, open journals), reading libraries used to look and not to cite, and sources never cited (AI summary pages, bookshop listings, blogs, Wikipedia prose). It also notes that Gemini's register says its URLs came from search outputs and that it extracted licence text for none of them, so none counts as opened. `docs/agents/source-families.md` points to it.
### Added
- **Seventeen more dictionaries in the Dictionaries Browser, from works 26 to 50 of the research list.** New records for the dictionaries of Qur'anic and hadith vocabulary (*ʿUmdat al-Ḥuffāẓ*, *al-Fāʾiq*, Abū ʿUbayd's *Gharīb al-Ḥadīth*), of legal vocabulary (*al-Mughrib*, *Taḥrīr alfāẓ al-Tanbīh*, *al-Zāhir*), of philology (*Fiqh al-lugha*, *al-Furūq al-lughawiyya*, *Dīwān al-adab*, *Durrat al-ghawwāṣ*), of loanwords (*al-Muʿarrab*, *Shifāʾ al-ghalīl*), of proverbs (*Majmaʿ al-amthāl*) and of the modern period (*Muḥīṭ al-muḥīṭ*, Wehr, Dozy, *al-Muʿjam al-wasīṭ*). Each states only what the TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi article says, with dates, editions and arrangement. Among the facts: *Fiqh al-lugha*'s second part was taken from Ibn Fāris's *al-Ṣāḥibī*, after which al-Thaʿālibī made the first part its own book; *Dīwān al-adab*'s supposed Yemen origin is a confusion; al-Muṭarrizī is stated as Muʿtazilī in creed and Ḥanafī in practice with that source named. Five author records are new (al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī, al-Muṭarrizī, Isḥāq al-Fārābī, Abū Hilāl al-ʿAskarī, Shihāb al-Dīn al-Khafājī); Wehr, Dozy and the Cairo Academy's dictionary are modern and in copyright, so they are described and linked, not hosted. The browser gains five more sections and seventeen more source records for the articles used.
### Added
- **Eleven more dictionaries in the Dictionaries Browser, each with facts checked against the TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi.** New records for *Tahdhīb al-Lugha*, *Jamharat al-Lugha*, *Maqāyīs al-Lugha*, *Mujmal al-Lugha*, *al-Mukhaṣṣaṣ*, *al-Nihāya*, *al-Taʿrīfāt* and *Kashshāf iṣṭilāḥāt al-funūn*, and the earlier cards for *al-Muḥkam*, *Asās al-Balāgha* and *al-Mufradāt* now carry their authors, dates, sources and arrangement. Each work links to its author and, where the encyclopaedia says so, to the dictionaries it draws on (for example *Kitāb al-ʿAyn* to *al-Jamhara*, *al-Maqāyīs* and *al-Muḥkam*). The browser gains three sections: thematic dictionaries, the vocabulary of the hadith, and technical terms. Twelve more source records name each encyclopaedia article, what it was used for and what it does not say.
- **The museum no longer states al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī's death date as fact.** The encyclopaedia entry says the date is very uncertain (classical sources give none; later ones range from 322 to 690 AH, and 502 AH does not fit other evidence it cites). The earlier catalogue's 502 AH is therefore not used; the record cites this source for the uncertainty.
- The museum's scholarly record, written down in the repository: the description paper — *islam.museum: A Citable Open Knowledge Graph and Digital Museum of Islamic History* — was published on Zenodo as a preprint (CC BY 4.0; cite all versions: 10.5281/zenodo.24273662; v1.0: 10.5281/zenodo.24273663), and the dataset record now links back to it (is described by, is cited by). The README gains a "Scholarly record and citation" section, a new engineering document (53 · Scholarly record) sets out the Zenodo archiving flow, the cite-the-concept-DOI policy and where it is implemented, the ORCID/DataCite link, and which indexes carry the dataset as verified on the day; the Cite page gains a section pointing researchers to the paper, and the whitepaper's deposit package in `docs/outreach/whitepaper-2026/` is stamped with its DOIs and marked published. The record was refreshed on 20 November 2026 against main of that day: the dataset's daily Zenodo versions now run to v2026.11.20 (10.5281/zenodo.24396188), and the index notes carry the 20 November re-check of the paper's record (14 views, 18 downloads as displayed that day).
- Wa Nalqa al-Ahibba, Amr Khaled (lecture series, Assabile archive): episodes 33, 34 and 35 added in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish drafts. Episode 33 is Zaynab bint Jahsh (her family, her brothers at Uhud, her marriage to Zayd ibn Harithah, the verses that ended adoption) and Juwayriya bint al-Harith and the Banu al-Mustaliq. Episode 34 is Safiyya bint Huyayy (the Jews of Medina, the dream, Khaybar, her marriage) and Umm Habiba's journey to Abyssinia and her marriage by proxy. Episode 35 is Maria the Copt (the letter to al-Muqawqis, Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a's journey, Ibrahim's birth and death) and Maymuna bint al-Harith, the last of the wives. Each statement is cited to the recording by timestamp; the speaker's dates and figures are marked as needing a source. Machine transcripts, not listened to.
### Changed
- **The UNESCO–Sharjah 2027 outreach papers now record the campaign as it stands on 20 November 2026, refreshed against main of the same day.** In `docs/outreach/unesco-2027/`, the endorsers list, the state of play, the letters and the eligibility memo now show: the founder sent L1, L2, L3 and the IRCICA thank-you himself on 15 November; Professor Hoyland declined on 16 November and that thread is closed, his earlier sentence standing as a personal remark only; Professor An-Na'im agreed to nominate and his signed page is awaited; the Prize Secretariat clarified the nominator rules on 18 November and signalled that the 30 November deadline is expected to be extended; IFLA, ICOMOS and the Muslim World League are parked, and the cold letters (Arab Thought Foundation, Arab British Centre, Professor Bahia Shehab, Biblioteca Islámica) were not sent. The papers now describe the museum as it stands on main today: Arabic first, with the English and Urdu editions live and the French and Spanish editions completed and merged on 19 November 2026, going live at the founder's next deployment; 81,578 entries across 250,362 record pages and 300 pathways on the live site as read on 19 November 2026; and Library and Archives Canada's completed full test crawl of the site (November 2026). Nothing has been filed; the papers say "seeking a nomination", as before.
- **The English Hudhud stories are all picture-books now, and the catalogue says so.** On 20 November 2026 the nine English episodes that were still cover-art videos (Episodes 2–10) were remade as flip picture-books in the first episode's manner — the same tellings, the same titles and the same descriptions, turned page by page — and took their places in the "Hudhud Bedtime Stories" playlist; the cover-art versions stay public on the channel, outside the playlist. The podcast catalogue (`docs/outreach/podcast-series.md`) now links each English episode to its picture-book video.
### Fixed
- **The IndexNow ping now names every sitemap file, read from the fresh sitemap index.** The script built its sitemap list from `/sitemap.xml` (or named only that file), and a copy of that file made during a deploy stayed in the edge cache for hours: after the production deploy of 20 November it listed 7 of the 11 sitemaps, so the newest ones, which hold the French and Spanish pages, were left out. Every mode of `scripts/indexnow.mjs` now reads `sitemap-index.xml` past the edge cache and submits `sitemap.xml` plus each file it lists (12 addresses today instead of 1 after a deploy); if the index cannot be read it names `sitemap.xml` only, as before, and the ping still goes. The production-only guard is unchanged. Also documented in `docs/indexnow.md`: the ping is a job of "Deploy all parts to production" and not of the standalone shared or language deploys.
- **The parts of the by-language build and deploy now do what the one build and the one deploy did that they had left out.** An audit of 21 November 2026 found four gaps. (1) `check:site` and `check:weight` ran in no by-language job; a new job `check (whole site)` puts the shared parts and the five languages together and runs both (on build 44761868478 they pass: 493,860 pages, 0 errors, 86 routes within budget), and the shared deploy refuses a run whose check failed. (2) The page count in the deploy stamp was copied from the previous live stamp: production said 279,334 pages while the site has 493,860, and the Backstage page shows that number; the same job now counts the pages and the shared deploy stamps the count (a run without it keeps the live count and warns). (3) IndexNow, which the one production deploy sent after publishing, is a job of "Deploy all parts to production" again, skipped when any part failed or the repository variable INDEXNOW is off. (4) The documentation states what is still different: no `seed` input, five-day artifacts and no pruning. The page count on production stays wrong until the next full deploy of a build that has the new job.
- **The R2 publish no longer fails on files too big for a Worker.** The UAT deploy of 20 November 2026 (run 44758556248) stopped in its second batch with "Memory limit would be exceeded before EOF": the sync Worker unpacks a whole archive in its 128 MB of memory, and the graph export `api/v1/graph/nodes.ndjson` has grown to 162 MB with the French and Spanish records. The publisher now uploads any file bigger than an archive's 20 MB cap (14 files in the shared build) straight to the bucket with the same S3 tool that stages the archives, with the Worker's own content types, and sends everything else through the Worker as before. The check against the Worker's allowed folders does not apply to these files, because their destinations come from the publish targets, not from outside input. A unit test pins the split. A build made after this change is needed, because the deploy runs the publisher from the built commit.
- **The test job of the by-language build no longer runs out of memory on a hosted runner.** Three builds of `main` in a row (runs 44736140498, 44738042244 and 44742628818) had their `test` job shut down by GitHub ("The runner has received a shutdown signal") two to three minutes into `npm test`, so no build could be deployed. The cause is the memory of the test files that load the compiled graph (549 MB of JSON, about 2 GB in memory each time; one worker was measured at 7.6 GB), which vitest ran three at a time on a 16 GB runner. When the CI variable is set, vitest now runs one test file at a time (`vitest.config.ts`); nothing is skipped and no assertion changed. The cost is a longer test job in CI; local runs keep every core.
- **The by-language build of `main` failed at its first step in the English, Urdu and Arabic jobs: the Ritha page imported `scripts/ritha` one folder level short.** The path in `site/src/pages/[lang]/ritha/[...page].astro` had four `../` where the file needs five (as the Places page has), so the build stopped with "Could not resolve" before building any page; it now resolves, and an English build gets past that step and generates pages. The browser registry also listed `mukatabat`, `munazarat`, `nar`, `nature`, `nubuwat` and `places` twice after the Juha and Ritha merges (the build warned "Duplicate key"); the second copy is removed, and `juha` stays.
- **The shared-parts deploy to UAT stopped at the podcast folder, and a guard now keeps that from happening again.** The sync Worker's list of folders it may write to (`ALLOWED_PREFIXES`) did not have `podcast/`, so the publish was refused with "destination not allowed" after the build had been found and thousands of files had been sent; `podcast/` is now allowed in both Worker environments and excluded from the Pages-only folder in the shared deploy, as it already was in the single deploy. A new test (`scripts/r2-registration.test.ts`) reads every place that decides where a data folder may go (the publisher, the site Worker's route list and run-first list, both Worker configs, the three deploy workflows' Pages excludes, the root-file rules) and checks every folder of `site/public` against them, so the next new folder fails in a pull request, not minutes into a deploy. The Workers are deployed from the built commit, so a build made after this change is needed before the deploy is started again.
- **Two Urdu strings of the Dictionaries Browser failed the Arabic-parentheses rule** (the pilot note and the Ṣiḥāḥ lede); they now wrap the Arabic parentheticals as the rule requires, and 
- **Verse topic labels removed from episodes 1 to 6 of How to Savour Prayer (Mishari al-Kharraz, Assabile archive).** In Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish, the fourteen bullets that named or restated what a Qur'anic verse says now use the neutral form already used for episodes 7 to 9: the speaker cites a verse, with no verse number given, and the verse is not written. The episode 3 report about the trust and the episode 4 account of Moses are worded the same way, so no verse wording is echoed. Cites and links are unchanged. The note on verses in the left-out list said "six episodes"; it now counts the nine episodes landed (1 to 9) in all five languages.

## v2.26.0 — 2026-11-20
### Added
- **The text of *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* is now in the museum, page by page.** The 1865 Būlāq printing, read with Apple Vision, is published as 1,228 records, one for each scan page of the two volumes (646 and 582; covers and library plates are left out). Each record cites its scan, shows the page text and says plainly that it is a machine reading: in a sample of six lines checked by eye against the page image, about one word in five had a wrong or split letter. `/{lang}/maajim/sihah/` lists the pages by volume. The text is not yet divided into entries and nothing beyond that sample has been checked. This follows the founder's ruling of 20 November 2026 (route A, then widened to all the pages), now written into `docs/sources-policy.md` and the decision inbox.
- **A signature view for the Dictionaries Browser: three doors to one root.** The browser's home draws the root ج ر ع filed three ways: by place of articulation in *Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, by last then first radical in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, and by first radical in *Asās al-Balāgha*; the Ṣiḥāḥ door links to the scan page where the root actually stands. The browser also has its own thumbnail on the main page, and stays in the Explore menu under Texts.
- **Page records of a dictionary show their text.** A `passage` of unit `other` now shows its text and its reliability note on its page; no other page changes.
### Data
- **Both volumes of the 1865 Bulaq *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* are now read in full (654 and 590 pages).** The Apple Vision reading of the second volume finished and the register records both outputs with their checksums. The text is still machine output, unchecked, and no entry from it is published yet.
### Added
- **A new browser for the most famous words of elegy and of announcing a death (`/{lang}/ritha/`, «متصفح أشهر ما قيل في الرثاء والنعي»).** It gathers 607 records from the Qur'an, the Sunnah, the seerah, the reports of the Companions and the Successors and the harvested books: the verses of patience, the Prophet's words «to God belongs what He took and what He gave» and «patience is at the first blow», his announcement of Ja'far, Zayd, Ibn Rawaha and the Negus, the condolences, Hassan's and Ka'b ibn Malik's elegies, and the limits of weeping and wailing. It opens with four mourning banners, a death-notice frame and the famous formulas; it is in the Explore menu, on the landing page, in the API (`/api/v1/ritha.json`), `llms.txt` and the OpenAPI file, in all five languages.
- **A new record, `concept/ritha-wal-nay`, with prose in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish,** and nineteen existing records on elegy, announcement, condolence and wailing filed into the browser.
### Data
- **395 passages harvested for the browser:** 74 reports from the seven hadith-api Arabic editions and 321 cited excerpts (at most 40 words, machine-read, not corrected) from 38 OCR'd books, each with its label and summary in five languages.
### Tests
- **The feature API test covers the new export** (`scripts/features-api.test.ts`): kinds, corpus sections, a book harvested later, and the three false-positive families (inheritance, source attribution, «نعت» the description).

## v2.25.0 — 2026-11-20
### Added
- **The Juha and Islamic Folklore Browser (متصفح جحا والفلكلور الإسلامي عبر العصور والكوميديا والنكت والطرائف والنوادر), at `/{lang}/juha/` in all five languages.** A new front door for humour in the Islamic tradition, requested by the founder on 20 November 2026: Juha and Nasreddin Hoca, the named wits and fools, the anecdote genre (nawadir), jesting, laughter and smiling, and the ethics of the joke — in the Qur'an, the Sunnah, the seerah, the reports of the Companions and Successors, and the harvested books. The page is a storyteller's gathering unlike any other browser: Juha riding his donkey backwards, the gathering of the wits as medallion seats, a strip of Juha's anecdotes as speech bubbles, a "scale of laughter" showing which kinds of humour each section carries, and the shelf of the anecdote books; below them, six sections with kind chips and a search box. It has a card on the homepage, an entry in the Explore menu, and its own data file at `/api/v1/juha.json` (documented in `docs/data/README.md`, the OpenAPI file and `llms.txt`). Passages are found at build time by a guarded detector (`scripts/juha.ts`), so every book harvested later brings its jokes here with no further work. The founder's brief is kept word for word in `docs/engineering/64-juha-browser-requirements.md` with twelve acceptance tests for production; the plan is `docs/plan/72-juha-browser.md`.
- **A new browser: the Rulings Browser — «متصفح الفروض والواجبات والطاعات والمستحبات والمكروهات والمحرمات وصغائر الذنوب» (`/[lang]/ahkam/`, plan 72, requested by the founder on 20 November 2026).** One front door for the degrees of obligation: the obligations, the obligation on every person (fard 'ayn) and on the community (fard kifaya), the acts of obedience, the obligatory, the recommended, the forbidden, the disliked, the minor sins, and what remains of the scale, the permitted and the concession. Its opening view is its own, "the scale of the five rulings": five degrees side by side from the act that must be done to the act that must be left, as al-Ghazali divides them in al-Mustasfa, each with the themes that stand on it. Ten theme pages open with a definition card from the books of usul. The build holds 4,607 records (`npx tsx scripts/ahkam-audit.ts`): 130 Qur'an ayahs, 2,500 Sunnah passages, 208 seerah excerpts, 1,735 excerpts from other books and 34 curated records; by theme (a record can carry more than one) 913 obligations, 180 individual obligation, 81 communal obligation, 237 obedience, 929 obligatory, 791 recommended, 1,774 forbidden, 478 disliked, 85 minor sins, 955 permitted and concession. Qur'an verses come from a reviewed table; other passages are found at build time by a guarded word list, so a book harvested later appears by itself; a bare prohibition is not classed as forbidden or disliked, because that is a jurist's reading. Six new records carry prose in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish (`concept/al-ahkam-al-taklifiyya`, `fard`, `fard-ayn`, `fard-kifaya`, `taa`, `haram-hukm`), with al-Shafi'i's account of the communal obligation cited to al-Risala. The browser has a card on the landing page, an entry in the Explore menu, the dataset `/api/v1/ahkam.json` and its acceptance checklist in `docs/engineering/64-ahkam-browser-requirements.md`. The museum describes what the texts and the jurists say and issues no ruling. Limits said plainly: the translations are machine-made and the excerpts from scanned books machine-read, none yet read by a person; the full build was not run before the merge, on the founder's instruction; the Explore menu entry changes every page at the next deploy (`rewrites-all-pages`).

### Data
- **Juha's anecdotes, one record each.** Every anecdote of *Nawadir Juha al-Kubra* (ed. Darwish al-Juwaydi) that passed the text rules is now its own passage record (`passage/nawadir-juha-<n>`): the printed Arabic title, a retelling in the museum's own words in Arabic, English, Urdu, French and Spanish, the page and number, and an excerpt of at most forty words. The retellings come from a machine-read scan that was not checked against the page images, and the translations are machine translations no human has read; each record says so.
- **Humour in the hadith collections and the books.** 150 reports of jesting, laughter, smiling and the limits of the joke from the seven hadith collections, and 644 cited excerpts from 24 scanned books — al-Nuwayri's *Nihayat al-Arab* (volume 4), Ibn Qutayba's *'Uyun al-Akhbar*, *al-Mustatraf*, al-Jahiz's *al-Bayan wa-l-Tabyin* and *al-Hayawan*, the *Ihya'*, and the seerah, Companion, biography and history books. Excerpts are chosen by vocabulary, so a few carry the word without being funny; the label says what was detected.
- **New and enriched records.** Four concepts — jesting (`concept/al-muzah`), laughter and smiling (`concept/al-dahik`), the anecdote (`concept/al-nawadir`) and the wits and the fools (`concept/al-zurafa-wa-al-mughaffalun`) — and first full prose in five languages for Juha, Nasreddin Hoca and *Nawadir Juha al-Kubra*, written from the edition's introduction with the editor's claims attributed to him and his contradictory dates for Nasreddin Hoca both given. A source record for the Cairo 1996 scan of *'Uyun al-Akhbar*. Twenty-three existing records (persons, works, places, a concept) carry the browser's tag. The Urdu title of *Nawadir Juha al-Kubra*, which a machine translation had misspelt, is corrected.
- **886 hadith reports and 1,368 book excerpts for the Rulings Browser** (lane `ahkam`): reports from the seven Arabic hadith-api editions and excerpts of at most forty words from 81 books already OCR'd on the harvest drive, led by the books of usul al-fiqh (al-Risala, al-Burhan, al-Mustasfa, al-Muwafaqat, Irshad al-Fuhul), each with labels and summaries in the five languages and a `mentions` edge to its theme's record. No book was downloaded and no PDF, OCR text or page image entered git.

### Tests
- **The browser's data file is tested** (`scripts/features-api.test.ts`): detection of each kind, the section of a Juha collection, a book that does not exist yet landing in "other books", and four false positives that must stay out («طرفة عين», «أرجحا», «الضحاك بن مزاحم», «ابن مغفل»).

## v2.24.0 — 2026-11-18
### Added
- **The by-language trial now covers the whole site, with one start for all of it.** The five language deploys published pages and search indexes only. Everything that belongs to no language now has its own build job and its own deploy: the API files, the shared data (media, maps, education files), the feed, `llms.txt`, the favicons, the scripts and styles, the site Worker and the Pages project. The sitemap is made by a small job that joins the five languages' own sitemaps with the same code the one build uses; in a sample build the result was the same file, byte for byte. Two new workflows, "Deploy all parts to UAT" and "Deploy all parts to production", take one build and run the shared deploy and then the five language deploys one after another. The one build and the one deploy are unchanged, and nothing of this has run on GitHub yet (`docs/engineering/06-deployment.md` section 9a).
- **A trial: the site can be built and published one language at a time.** The one build writes all five languages on a single GitHub machine, which is more than that machine's documented disk holds, and the build of 18 November on the Spanish release branch stopped that way. A new workflow, started by hand, builds each language on its own machine, five at once, and keeps each language's pages and search index as its own package. Ten new deploy workflows, five for production and five for UAT, publish one language's pages and search index and leave everything else on the site as it is: the other languages, the API, the sitemap, the shared scripts and styles. The existing build and the two existing deploys are unchanged and are still the only way to publish the whole site. Limits a reader should know: a language published alone can be out of step with the others (its language switch may lead to a page another language does not have yet), and the two whole-site checks do not run on a language build. Checked on the founder's Mac with a sample build (about 10,400 pages per language, not the full site): every Spanish page and the Spanish search index of a Spanish-only build are byte-for-byte what the full build writes. Not yet run on GitHub, and nothing has been deployed with it (`docs/engineering/06-deployment.md` section 9).
- **Spanish (`es`) as the fifth language of the museum — infrastructure and interface (branch `release/spanish`, proposal `docs/delegation/spanish-language-proposal.md`).** The site now builds `/es/` beside `/ar/`, `/en/`, `/ur/` and `/fr/`: the language switcher cycles ar → en → ur → fr → es, each page carries a Spanish hreflang alternate, a `pagefind-es` search index is built, and the site Worker, the R2 publish list and the deploy workflow know the new folders. `i18n/es.yaml` carries the interface in Spanish, translated from `i18n/en.yaml` by AI agents and not yet read by a human; dates, eras and month names have Spanish forms. What a visitor does **not** get yet: no record has Spanish prose, labels or summaries, and the education, kids and tour datasets have no Spanish fields, so those show English (then Arabic) inside the Spanish frame; passage pages have no Spanish translation of the Qur'an (no source is chosen). Spanish stays outside the parity requirements (`PUBLISHED_LANGS`) until its corpus lands, and no language count in `docs/status.md`, the site copy or the outreach files is changed. The `spanish` lane (`docs/agents/lanes/spanish.md`, queue `scripts/es-queue.ts`, progress `docs/delegation/spanish-progress.md`) carries the corpus work, in parallel with the French lane. The language rule in `AGENTS.md` and `docs/language.md` now names Spanish for new content. Nothing is live: `release/spanish` is not merged to `main` and nothing is deployed.
### Added
- **The museum opens in the visitor's own language.** Someone who arrives at the bare address `islam.museum/` is now taken to the museum in their browser's default language when that language is English, Urdu, French or Spanish; Arabic speakers, speakers of any other language, and browsers without JavaScript get the Arabic page the root has always served. Only the root does this: `/ar/`, `/en/` and every deeper address stay where they are, so choosing a language in the header is never undone. A language chosen in the header is remembered: the next visit to the root opens in that language, whatever the browser's own language, until the visitor chooses another. The only thing kept is that language code, in the visitor's own browser storage, never sent anywhere (the privacy page lists it); search-engine crawlers are left on the Arabic root. The change lives in one shared script file (`site/public/shell/shell.js`), so no page is rewritten.

- **A research prompt for the planned Dictionaries Browser (`docs/delegation/gemini/dictionaries-browser-prompt-b-history.md`).** It asks Gemini for the history, manuscripts, printings, reception and controversies of 40 classical Arabic dictionaries and of their authors, in seven batches, with every claim sourced and unverifiable items marked. It also records what two earlier rounds of research found about where the texts can lawfully come from. Nothing is built or published; the answers will be checked before any record is written.

- **A written proposal for the Dictionaries Browser (`docs/plan/72-dictionaries-browser.md`).** It sets out what the browser holds (the dictionaries, their authors, their sources, and entries readable in full), the first run of 40 works, what two rounds of research established about where texts can lawfully come from, and the one decision still open: where the readable text comes from. It also records that the museum's own scans of *Lisān al-ʿArab*, *al-Qāmūs* and *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* are too noisy to display. Nothing is built.
- **The Dictionaries Browser starts: «متصفح المعاجم» at `/{lang}/maajim/`.** A new page in all five languages lists the museum's records of the great dictionaries in sections (general dictionaries of Arabic, the vocabulary of the Qur'an, geographic dictionaries), with each work's author, and explains where the text of a dictionary will and will not be shown. Nine dictionary records are in it in this first batch, among them *Lisān al-ʿArab*, *Kitāb al-ʿAyn*, *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, *al-Qāmūs al-Muḥīṭ* and *Tāj al-ʿArūs*; the five general ones now carry dates, named sources and their arrangement, each taken from the Turkish TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi and cited on the record (for example that Ibn Manẓūr finished *Lisān al-ʿArab* on 22 Dhū l-Ḥijja 689 AH, 26 December 1290, from five named earlier dictionaries). The whole list is also available as `/api/v1/maajim.json`, is documented in `docs/site/browsers.md`, `site/public/openapi/v1.json` and `llms.txt`, and is found by search.
- **Eight encyclopaedia source records and two scan records for the dictionaries.** Each TDV article that a record relies on is its own source record, with what it was used for and what it does not say (two of them are short cross-references and are used only for one fact each). The two scan records describe the Bulaq 1282 AH / 1865 printing of *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* held by the Internet Archive, which the archive itself marks as not in copyright, with the file sizes and checksums of the copies the museum downloaded.
- **A pilot for reading a dictionary in full.** The two volumes of the 1865 Bulaq *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* were downloaded and volume 1 is being read with Apple Vision; on a test page the result is far cleaner than the museum's older scans of the same book but still contains errors, so no entry is published yet. The browser page says so, and each entry will show its page and how accurately it was read. The founder chose this route (a pilot from a pre-1925 print, with other dictionaries linked, not copied) on 20 November 2026.


### Tests
- **The test suite runs again after the Spanish and French pages arrived (`scripts/build-graph.test.ts`).** One test file validated the whole repository and also compiled the whole graph twice. With 12,700 more pages the compiled graph alone holds about 3 GB, and the test process ran out of memory, on the build machine and on a laptop alike. The graph tests now have their own file and compile the graph once; the same assertions run, none was dropped and no memory limit was raised.

### Added
- **The Qur'an can be read with a French and a Spanish translation.** A verse page and the sura reader showed a translation of the verse in English (Pickthall) and Urdu (Jalandhari) only. French readers now see Rachid Maach's translation and Spanish readers Muhammad Isa García's, both as published by QuranEnc.com (versions 1.0.3 and 1.0.2), with their footnotes, the translator's name, the version and a link to the source. No French or Spanish translation accepted among Sunni institutions is in the public domain, so these two are shown under QuranEnc.com's own terms: unchanged, credited, with the version stated. They are third-party content, not CC0: they are kept in their own files, outside the museum's data, the frozen Qur'an records and the open API (`docs/data/quran-translations.md`). The Arabic text is untouched. Founder's decision, 20 November 2026.

### Fixed
- **The courses are now built in French and Spanish too, and their language links work.** The course and lesson pages were written for Arabic, English and Urdu only, while every one of them offered a French and a Spanish version and the French and Spanish course index listed all 65 courses: 2,686 links to pages that did not exist, which the link check of the full build caught. The lesson text and the interface strings for both languages were already complete, so the pages are now built: 426 more in each language. Course and lesson titles still appear in English there, because the records carry no French or Spanish labels yet.

The headings are now «Pour les jeunes visiteurs», «Pour les plus jeunes visiteurs» and «Notes pour les chercheurs», as in the rest of the French pages; the text under them is unchanged. `npm run validate` is back to 0 errors.
- **A link to the hadith narrator Ibn Hamas is whole again in Spanish** (`passage/muwatta-31-2597`): the machine translation had put only «Ibn» inside the link, which also tripped the content-safety check on the bare second word.
- **A Spanish viewpoint block may open with any Sunni label that contains «suní» or «suníes»** (`scripts/validate.ts`), not only one that starts with it, and never one that says «no suní».
- **Episode 4 of "Hudhud's Story Time" in the podcast feed now points to a repaired recording.** The first published audio of "The Woman Who Built a University" was faulty: partway through, the narration fell into a repeating loop and never delivered the middle of the story. The episode has been re-recorded with the same script and the same two voices, checked in full against the script, and the feed entry now carries the new recording (2:41 instead of the faulty 6:18). Anyone who downloaded the old file has the loop; the feed itself now serves the repaired episode.

### Data

They had been left out of the Spanish and French translation until he ruled; he ruled that they are translated like the rest. Their prose pages are now in Spanish and French and their titles and summaries in Urdu, French and Spanish, by the same route as the other records. Each translation was compared with its English source: none names a blocked organisation the English does not. The ruling is recorded in `docs/delegation/extremism-firewall-exceptions.md`. Those records were reviewed one by one by the founder and are no precedent for new content, and their prose has been held from translation for his ruling; the same now holds for their titles and summaries. ### Data
- **Record titles and summaries in Urdu: 70,339 more texts in about 43,400 records.** Two records in five had an Urdu title and summary; now nearly all do. Translated from English by Google Translate's document translation (two files uploaded by the founder), checked by script; blessing formulas the machine added were removed; 463 names it left in Latin letters are still missing. The frozen Qur'an passage records and the held records are untouched. Machine translation, not read by a human.

They were translated from English by Google Translate's document translation (four files uploaded by the founder) and checked by script, with the same choices as for Spanish: person names keep their English transliteration, titles of sources are left as published, the frozen Qur'an passage records are untouched. Machine translation, not read by a human.
